items.e: Yes; for all true obedience, is "the obedience of faith," Rom. 16:26, and "without faith it is impossible to please God," Heb. 11:6.

items.h: In what manner are we required to worship and glorify God?
items.e: Both inwardly in our hearts, John 4:24, and outwardly in our lives, Matt. 5:16.

items.h: How are we to worship God inwardly in our hearts?
items.e: By trusting, Isaiah 26:4; hoping, Psalm 130:5, and delighting in him, Psalm 37:4; by thinking and meditating upon him, Mal. 3:16, Psalm 63; devoting ourselves to him, Isaiah 44:5; and by being filled with grief, when he is offended by ourselves or others, Psalm 38:18, and 119:136.

items.h: How are we to worship and glorify him outwardly in our lives?
items.e: By praying to him, and praising him with our lips, Psalm 142:1, and 145:21; by being zealous for his glory, Psalm 69:9; careful to please him, Col. 1:10; and by walking humbly before him, Micah. 6:8.

items.h: What improvement ought we to make of the covenant grant in the preface, I am the Lord thy God; and the precept enjoining the belief of this, Thou shalt have no other gods before me?
items.e: That it is the duty of every one of us, without waiting till we find gracious qualifications wrought in us, instantly to lay claim to a God in Christ, as our God, Psalm 95:7; this being what he requires in the first place, as the foundation of all other acts of obedience, 2 Chron. 20:20.

items.h: If it is an external federal relation to the visible church, which God asserts in the preface, when he says, I am the Lord thy God, how can the First Commandment warrant the faith of a special relation?
items.e: As the command always warrants a particular application of every general promise, so the external federal relation which God bears to the visible church, becomes a special one, the moment that the promise is believed with a particular applicatory faith, Jer. 3:22.

items.h: What is forbidden in the First Commandment?
items.e: The First Commandment forbiddeth the denying, or not worshipping and glorifying the true God, as God and our God; and the giving that worship and glory to any other which is due to him alone.

items.h: To what general heads may the sins forbidden, in the First Commandment, be reduced?
items.e: To these two: atheism and idolatry.

items.h: What is A THEISM?
items.e: It is the denying, or not having a God.

items.h: How is atheism commonly distinguished?
items.e: Into speculative and practical.

items.h: How is speculative atheism again subdivided?
items.e: Into that which is directly, and that which is interpretatively such.

items.h: What is direct speculative atheism?
items.e: It is a fixed persuasion in the heart, and an open profession with the mouth, that there is no God.

items.h: What is speculative atheism, interpretatively, or by necessary consequence?
items.e: It is the rejection of any of those truths which are necessarily connected with the being of a God; such as the denial of providence, or any of the essential perfections of God: because from thence it would necessarily follow, that there is no God.

items.h: Why would it necessarily follow, from the denial of providence, or any of the divine perfections, that there is no God?
items.e: Because it is impossible to conceive that there is a God, without conceiving, at the same time, that he preserves and governs the world, Isaiah 41; and it is impossible to conceive his being or existence, without conceiving him to be possessed of all infinite perfection, 1 John 1:5.

items.h: Can there be such a person among men, as a direct speculative atheist?
items.e: No; there can be none of mankind, who has, at all times, such a fixed and constant persuasion that there is no God, as at no time whatsoever to have the least fear or doubt of the contrary, Dan. 5:6, 9.

items.h: How does it appear that there can be no such person as a downright speculative atheist?
items.e: From universal experience, which attests, that the knowledge and impression of the being of a God, is so natural to man, that he can no more divest himself of it at all times, than he can strip himself of his reason, or shake off his own existence, Rom. 1:19 - "That which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath showed it unto them:" that is, ingrained it in their natures.

items.h: Would it not seem, that there may be a downright speculative atheist, from Psalm 14:1 - "The fool hath said in his heart, there is no God?"
items.e: The words do not import a fixed and permanent persuasion, but rather a secret wish: accordingly, the expression is not, The fool hath believed, or is persuaded in his heart, but hath said: that is, would fain have harboured such a secret desire.

items.h: Why do wicked men wish there were no God?
items.e: To be free of any check or restraint upon their lusts, and that they may "work all uncleanness with greediness," Eph. 4:19.

items.h: Who are they that are interpretatively atheists?
items.e: Not only they who deny the providence of God, or any essential attribute of his nature, but likewise all deists, who reject supernatural revelation; and all openly wicked and profane persons, who live as if there was no God, Psalm 10:4, 11, 13.

items.h: Is it speculative or practical atheism, that chiefly levelled against, in this commandment?
items.e: Both: but especially practical atheism, as being universally prevalent, Rom. 3:11.

items.h: What is practical atheism?
items.e: It is a denial of God, in our practice, Titus 1:16 - "They profess that they know God, but in works they deny him."

items.h: How does practical atheism evidence itself?
items.e: In omitting the duties required in this commandment; namely, not knowing and acknowledging God to be what he really is, and neglecting to worship and glorify him accordingly.

items.h: Who are guilty of not knowing God?
items.e: Not only heathens, who walk contrary to nature's light, Rom. 1:21; but likewise Christians, who being privileged with the means of knowing God, as in Christ, yet slight and neglect the same; John 15:22 - "If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin; but now they have no cloak for their sin."

items.h: Who are they that are guilty of not acknowledging God?
items.e: They who rush upon the actions of life, without asking his counsel about them, Josh. 9:14 - "The men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the Lord."

items.h: Who are guilty of not worshipping God?
items.e: They who live in the habitual neglect of the public, private, and secret exercises of his worship, Isaiah 43:22 - "Thou hast not called upon me, O Jacob; thou hast been weary of me, O Israel."

items.h: Who are guilty of not glorifying God?
items.e: They who set up themselves as their own rule, Psalm 12:4, and make themselves their own end and happiness, in opposition to God, Phil. 2:21.

items.h: When are men chargeable with this piece of practical atheism; namely, of setting themselves up as their own rule?
items.e: When they perform any action, religious or civil, more because it is agreeable to self, than as it is pleasing to God, Zech. 7:5, 6; when they envy the gifts and prosperity of others, Psalm 73:3, and when they would model or frame God himself according to their own fancy, imagining him to be "altogether such a one as themselves," Psalm 50:21.

items.h: When do men make themselves their own end and happiness in opposition to God?
items.e: When they ascribe the glory of what they have or do, to themselves, and not to God, Dan. 4:30; when they are more troubled for what disgraces themselves, than for what dishonours God, 1 Sam. 15:30; and when they prefer the pleasures and profits of this world, to the glorifying and enjoying of God, Matt. 19:22.

items.h: When may we be said to worship the true God, and yet not as God?
items.e: When we draw nigh to him with the mouth, and honour him with our lips, but our hearts are far from him, Matt. 15:8.

items.h: When are we guilty of not worshipping and glorifying him, as our God?
items.e: When, in the course or tenor of our behaviour and deportment towards him, we want the habitual exercise of the faith of our federal relation to him, Psalm 81:10, 11.

items.h: May not the saints themselves be chargeable with some degree of practical atheism?
items.e: No doubt they may; when they entertain unbecoming thoughts of God in their mind, or speak unadvisedly to him with their lips. Thus Job is censured by Elihu, for charging God with injustice, chap. 33:10, 11; and Jonah speaks most rashly to God, when he says, "I do well to be angry, even unto death," chap. 4:9.

items.h: How may a person know when blasphemous thoughts, and atheistical expressions, are not inconsistent with a state of grace?
items.e: When a blasphemous thought is so far from being indulged, that it is treated with abhorrence; and when an atheistical expression (uttered through surprise, and the hurry and violence of temptation) is deeply regretted and lamented, Psalm 73:21, 22.

items.h: What is the other general and comprehensive sin forbidden in this commandment?
items.e: IDO:ATRY.

items.h: What is idolatry?
items.e: It is the giving that worship and glory to any other, which is due to God alone.

items.h: How is idolatry commonly distinguished?
items.e: Into that which is gross and external, and that which is more refined and internal.

items.h: What is the idolatry which is gross and external?
items.e: It is an ascription of the ordinary signs of worship, or religious homage, to any person or thing, besides the true God, Lev. 26:1.

items.h: Who are they that are guilty of this grosser kind of idolatry?
items.e: HEATHENS and PAPISTS.

items.h: What was the nature of the idolatry of the Heathens?
items.e: They made gods of the sun, moon, and stars, and of almost every other creature; yea, of devils themselves, as the apostle witnesses, 1 Cor. 10:20. But that which was most frequent among them, was their making images or idols in the shape of some sort of living creatures, or of a mixture of them, and then worshipping them as if they were gods, Psalm 135:15-19.

items.h: How did Heathenish Idolatry take its rise in the world?
items.e: By men becoming "vain in their imaginations, whereby they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things," Rom. 1:21, 23.

items.h: How does it appear that the Papists are guilty of this grosser kind of idolatry?
items.e: By their bowing to images and altars; giving divine honour to the consecrated bread in the sacrament; adoring the crucifix; praying to angels; invoking the saints, especially the virgin Mary, whom they supplicate much more frequently than they do Christ himself. By all which it appears, that Popish idolatry succeeds in the room of the Heathenish; and is more inexcusable than theirs, because those who practise it have the benefit of divine revelation which the heathens have not.

items.h: How do you prove, that the paying religious homage to such things is gross idolatry?
items.e: From the nature of idolatry itself; the very essence of which consists in giving divine worship and honour to any creature whatsoever, whether in heaven or earth; for it is written, "Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve," Matt. 4:10.

items.h: What is the idolatry which is more refined and internal?
items.e: It is a setting up of idols in the heart, Ezek. 14:4; or giving that room in our esteem and affection to any thing else, which God alone ought to possess, Luke 14:26.

items.h: To whom is this kind of idolatry incident?
items.e: To all mankind naturally; and even believers themselves are cautioned and warned against it, 1 John 5:21 - "Little children, keep yourselves from idols."

items.h: What are these idols which have a seat in every man's and woman's heart by nature?
items.e: Among many others, there are these two; which are worshipped and served by the generality, even of the visible church, namely, SELF and the WORLD.

items.h: How does it appear that SELF is an idol which naturally reigns in the heart of every one?
items.e: From the very first lesson in the school of Christianity, which is, to deny self, Matt. 16:24 - "Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself."

items.h: What is it for a man to deny himself?
items.e: It is to give up with his self-wisdom, his self-will, and his self-righteousness.

items.h: When do we give up with the idol of self-wisdom?
items.e: When we are made to see our own depraved reason to be but folly, when compared with the wisdom of God revealed in his word; "for the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God," 1 Cor. 3:19.

items.h: When is the idol of self-will dethroned?
items.e: When God's will of precept becomes the sole rule of our heart and life, Psalm 119:105; and his will of providence is cheerfully acquiesced in as the best for us, Rom. 8:28.

items.h: When do we part with the idol of self-righteousness?
items.e: When we submit to the righteousness of God, or found our plea, for eternal life wholly and entirely upon the meritorious obedience and satisfaction of Christ, as our Surety, in our room and stead, Phil. 3:8, 9.

items.h: How does it appear that the WORLD is an idol seated in every man's heart by nature?
items.e: From the habitual turn of our thoughts and affections to things temporal, Matt. 6:31; the eager pursuit of them, and ardent desire after them, in preference to those that are spiritual and eternal, chap. 16:26.

items.h: What are the things of this world which we naturally incline to idolise?
items.e: Some make an idol of their worldly riches; making gold their hope, and saying to the fine gold, "Thou art my confidence," Job 31:24; some, of their worldly pleasures, being "lovers of pleasures, more than lovers of God," 2 Tim. 3:4; some make an idol of their worldly credit and reputation, receiving "honour one of another," and not seeking "the honour that cometh from God only," John 5:44; some, of their worldly relations bestowing more of their love upon them, than upon God, Matt. 10:37; and some make an idol of their worldly helps and confidences, trusting more to these than to God, Isaiah 31:1; Jer. 17:5.

items.h: What is the verdict of the Spirit of God concerning those who make the world their idol?
items.e: It is this, that "if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him," 1 John 2:15.

items.h: How may Satan be said to be even idolised by those who profess to bear him an implacable hatred?
items.e: When his suggestions are regarded more than the dictates of the Spirit of God in his word, Isaiah 40:27; 49:14.

items.h: How may the suggestions of Satan be distinguished from the dictates of the Spirit of God?
items.e: The tendency of all Satan's suggestions is to set up in the soul some one thing or other in Christ's room, 2 Cor. 4:4; but the dictates of the Spirit of God are wholly calculated for giving Christ in all things the pre-eminence, John 16:14.

items.h: Why is Satan called the God of this world? 2 Cor. 4:4.
items.e: Because he is "the spirit that worketh in the children of disobedience," Eph. 2:2, till "the prey be taken from the mighty, and the lawful captive delivered," Isaiah 49:24, 25.

items.h: Who are they that explicitly acknowledge the devil as their God?
items.e: They are such as use sorcery, divination, witchcraft, charms, and other diabolical arts and practices, condemned in Deut. 18:10-12.

items.h: Was Joseph's cup an instrument of divination, or did he himself use this unlawful art, when he says, Gen. 44:15 - "Wot ye not that such a man as I can certainly divine?"
items.e: By no means; for the word translated DIVINE is, on the margin, rendered make trial, or inquiry; and so the meaning is, Know ye not that such a man as I, who am so diligent and industrious in other matters, would soon miss the cup in which I usually drink, and make inquiry after the person who had stolen it?

items.h: What improvement ought we to make of the First Commandment, as it stands connected with the preface?
items.e: That as God warrants and commands us to believe in him, as our God and Redeemer, Psalm 45:11; so it is our duty to carry along with us the faith of this relation, in all our approaches to his presence, Heb. 11:6.

items.h: What are we especially taught by these words BEFORE ME in the First Commandment?
items.e: These words before me in the First Commandment, teach us, That God, who seeth all things, taketh notice of, and is much displeased with, the sin of having any other god.

items.h: What is the strength of the argument implied in these words before me?
items.e: That the sin of having any other god, is committed in the presence of him, who seeth all things, Heb. 4:13.

items.h: What is it for God to see all things?
items.e: It is to have a most intimate, perfect, and comprehensive knowledge of them, Psalm 147:5 - "His understanding is infinite."

items.h: In what consists the infinity of God's knowledge?
items.e: Not so much in the perfect and comprehensive knowledge of the creatures, which are finite; as in the perfect and comprehensive knowledge of himself, and his own excellencies and perfections, which are infinite, 1 Cor. 2:11.

items.h: How is it that God sees, or knows all things?
items.e: He sees all things at once in his own essence, distinctly, infallibly, and immutably, 1 John 1:5.

items.h: How do you prove that God has such a comprehensive sight and knowledge of all things?
items.e: Because otherwise he could not be the Creator, Governor, and Judge of the world, 1 Cor. 4:5.

items.h: In what light does God see or know evil actions?
items.e: As they are opposite to his nature, Jer. 44:4, and contrary to his law, 1 John 3:4, which is the sole and unerring standard of all rectitude, Rom. 7:12.

items.h: What is that sin which strikes more immediately and directly against the authority of God in this commandment?
items.e: It is the sin of having any other god.

items.h: What is it to have another god?
items.e: It is to have our minds, wills, and affections carried out after other objects, as much, or more than after God himself, Isaiah 46:9, compared with Ezek. 14:4.

items.h: What notice does God take of this sin?
items.e: He threatens to resent it with the highest marks of displeasure, and that even in this life, as well as in the world to come, Deut. 29:24-29.

items.h: Why is God so much displeased with the sin of having any other God?
items.e: Because it sets up a rival or competitor in his room, and that in his very sight and presence, Jer. 32:30.

items.h: What influence ought the presence of an all-seeing God to have upon us in all our actions?
items.e: The consideration of this ought to quicken and animate us to every duty, Gen. 5:22, 24; and affright and deter us from every sin, as being an affronting of him to his face, who is our witness, and ere long will be our judge, Gen. 39:9.

items.h: Which is the Second Commandment?
items.e: The Second Commandment is, Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the Lord thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me; and showing mercy unto thousands of them that love me and keep my commandments.:

items.h: What is required in the Second Commandment?
items.e: The Second Commandment requireth the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath appointed in his word.

items.h: What is the opinion of the Papists respecting this commandment?
items.e: They allege that it is not a distinct precept from the first, but only an appendix, or supplement to it, by way of illustration.

items.h: What is their practice, in consequence of this opinion?
items.e: They constantly leave it out in their mass books and other liturgies of their church, lest the people should observe the manifest contrariety of their image worship, to what is here so expressly forbidden.

items.h: In what then does the Second Commandment differ from the first?
items.e: The First Commandment respects the object, and requires that we worship the true God for our God, and no other: the second respects the means of worship, and requires that the true God be worshipped in such a way only, and by such ordinances as he has appointed in his word, in opposition to all human inventions.

items.h: What is meant by religious worship?
items.e: That homage and respect we owe to a gracious God, as a God of infinite perfection; by which we profess subjection to, and confidence in him, as our God in Christ, for the supply of all our wants; and ascribe the praise and glory that is due to him, as our chief good, and only happiness, Psalm 95:6, 7.

items.h: What are these religious ordinances, which God has appointed in his word?
items.e: They are "prayer and thanksgiving in the name of Christ; the reading, preaching, and hearing of the word, the administration and receiving of the sacraments; church government and discipline; the ministry and maintenance thereof; religious fasting; swearing by the name of God; and vowing to him."

items.h: Is prayer a moral duty founded in the law of nature?
items.e: It certainly is; the necessary dependence of the rational creature upon its Creator, plainly proves it to be so. Hence we find the very Heathens practising it, when reduced to straits, Jonah 1:14.

items.h: How does it appear to be an instituted means of worship?
items.e: From a variety of scripture texts enjoining the practice of it, in all cases and circumstances, Psalm 50:15; Phil. 4:6; 1 Thess. 5:17.

items.h: What is acceptable prayer?
items.e: It is an asking in Christ's name, what God has promised to give, John 14:13; with a full persuasion that he hears, and will answer, Mark 11:24; James 1:6.

items.h: How manifold is religious thanksgiving?
items.e: TWOFOLD; stated and occasional.

items.h: What is stated thanksgiving?
items.e: It is not only the thankful acknowledgment of mercies daily received, which is a branch of prayer; but likewise the singing the praises of God with the voice, which is a stated act of worship, distinct from prayer, though ejaculatory prayer ought always to be joined with it, Psalm 57:7.

items.h: How do you prove that singing with the voice is a stated act of worship appointed under the New Testament?
items.e: From the example of Christ and his apostles, who, after the first supper, sang a hymn, (or psalm, as on the margin,) Matt. 26:30; and from the injunction laid upon all Christians to be employed in this exercise, as a stated duty, Eph. 5:18, 19; James 5:13.

items.h: What should be the subject matter of our praises to God?
items.e: The psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, which are dictated by the Spirit of God in scripture; and not any human composure whatever, Eph. 5:19.

items.h: In what manner should these be sung?
items.e: "With grace in our hearts to the Lord," Col. 3:16.

items.h: What is it to sing with grace in our hearts to the Lord?
items.e: It is to have our hearts going along with our voice, in suitable acts of faith, and elevated affections, Psalm 57:7.

items.h: Are not the Psalms of David, as we sing them in our language, of human composure?
items.e: The translation in metre is human, but the sense and meaning are the same as the original.

items.h: What is occasional thanksgiving?
items.e: It is the setting some time apart for giving thanks to God, on account of some remarkable mercy and deliverance, respecting either churches and nations in general, Neh. 12:27; or ourselves and families in particular, Eph. 5:20.

items.h: How ought we to engage in this duty?
items.e: With an humble sense of our utter unworthiness of the least of all God's favours, 2 Sam. 7:18.

items.h: Are reading, hearing, and preaching of the word, acts of worship?
items.e: Although they are not acts of such immediate worship as prayer and praise, in which God is immediately addressed; yet being the instituted and ordinary means of salvation, they ought to be practised and attended with that reverence and regard which is due to the great God our Saviour, who is present in them, Matt. 28:20; Acts 10:33.

items.h: How are the administration and receiving of the sacraments acts of worship?
items.e: As in them, by the sensible signs of divine appointment, Christ, and his benefits, are represented, sealed, and applied to believers, Gal. 3:26; 1 Cor. 11:26.

items.h: In what sense are church government and discipline to be ranked among the ordinances of divine worship?
items.e: In as far as they are exercised in the name of the Lord Jesus, the alone head of the church, according to the rule of his word, by church judicatories lawfully constituted, Matt. 18:20.

items.h: Why are the ministry and the maintenance of it placed among religious ordinances?
items.e: Because, as a standing ministry in the church, till the end of time, is of express divine institution, Eph. 4:11-13; so the suitable and comfortable maintenance of it, is as expressly appointed, not only in the Old Testament, Num. 18:21, 24; but likewise in the New, 1 Cor. 9:13, 14 - "Do ye not know, that they which minister about holy things, live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar, are partakers with the altar? Even so hath the Lord ordained, that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel."

items.h: What is religious fasting?
items.e: "A religious fast requires total abstinence, not only from all food, (unless bodily weakness do manifestly disable from holding out, till the fast be ended,) but also from all worldly labour, discourses, and thoughts, and from all bodily delights."64 Josh. 7:6; Judges 20:26.

items.h: Is bodily fasting, or bare abstinence from food, any part of religious worship?
items.e: Not properly in itself; but as it is a mean of divine appointment, for fitting and disposing us for more spiritual and solemn exercises.

items.h: How does fasting appear to be a mean of divine appointment?
items.e: From the practice of the saints under the Old Testament, Esth. 4:16; Dan. 10:2, 3; from the testimony of Christ, Matt. 6:17, 18, and 17:21; and the example of his apostles under the New, Acts 13:3; and 14:23.

items.h: What are those spiritual and solemn exercises for which fasting is designed to dispose us?
items.e: Deep humiliation of soul before the Lord on account of sin, Ezra 9:6; free confession of it, Dan. 9:20, and turning from it, Joel 2:12, as the genuine fruits of our taking hold of God's covenant, Jer. 50:4, 5; together with an importunate requesting of our gracious God, for that which is the particular occasion of the fast, Psalm 35:13.

items.h: Is religious fasting an occasional or a stated duty?
items.e: It is merely occasional and extraordinary, to be observed as the call of Providence may require and direct.

items.h: What are the occurrences in providence, which are a call to this extraordinary duty?
items.e: "When some great and notable judgments are either inflicted upon a people," Dan. 9:3, 12-14, "or apparently imminent," 2 Chron. 20:2-4; "or, by some extraordinary provocations notoriously deserved," 1 Sam. 7:3, 6; "as also when some special blessing is to be sought and obtained,"65 ver. 5, 8, 10.

items.h: Is swearing by the name of God an act of immediate and instituted worship?
items.e: It is undoubtedly: and that either when we devote ourselves to God in a covenant of duties, Deut. 6:13, or declare the truth upon oath, when called thereto: because, in both cases the name of God is solemnly interposed and invoked, Jer. 4:2.

items.h: To whom are vows to be made?
items.e: To God alone, as the only party and witness in the making and performing of them, Psalm 76:11 - "Vow and pay unto the LORD your GOD."

items.h: What should be the subject matter of our vows to God?
items.e: Nothing except what may tend either to promote the practice of commanded duty, Psalm 119:57, or prevent the commission of any sin to which we are more ordinarily inclined and addicted, verse 106.

items.h: What does this commandment require, with respect to all those ordinances, and parts of worship, which God has appointed in his word?
items.e: The receiving and observing them; and keeping them pure and entire.

items.h: What is it to receive God's ordinances?
items.e: It is to approve of, and embrace them, as bearing the stamp of his authority upon them, Psalm 84:1, 2.

items.h: What is it to observe them?
items.e: It is to set about the practice of them, or to be actually employed in them, Psalm 55:17, and 119:164; Luke 2:37.

items.h: What is it to keep the ordinances of God pure?
items.e: It is to contribute our utmost endeavour to preserve them from all mixture of human invention, Deut. 12:32.

items.h: What is it to keep them entire?
items.e: It is, in the exercise of faith, to attend upon each of them in its proper season, so as that one duty may not jostle out another, Luke 1:6.

items.h: What does God require of us in this command, with reference to all false worship?
items.e: He requires "the disapproving, detesting, opposing all false worship, Psalm 16:4; and according to each one's place and calling, removing it, and all monuments of idolatry, Deut. 7:5."66:

items.h: What is forbidden in the Second Commandment?
items.e: The Second Commandment forbiddeth the worshipping of God by images, or any other way not appointed in his word.

items.h: What are the leading sins forbidden in this commandment?
items.e: Idolatry and will-worship.

items.h: What is the idolatry here condemned?
items.e: The worshipping of God by images: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image," &c.

items.h: What is an image?
items.e: It is a statue, picture, or likeness of any creature whatever.

items.h: Is it lawful to have images or pictures of mere creatures?
items.e: Yes, provided they be only for ornament; or the design be merely historical, to transmit the memory of persons and their actions to posterity.

items.h: Can any image or representation be made of God?
items.e: No; it is absolutely impossible; he being an infinite, incomprehensible Spirit, Isaiah 40:18 - "To whom will ye liken God? or, what likeness will ye compare unto him?" If we cannot delineate our own souls, much less the infinite God; Acts 17:29 - "We ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device."

items.h: What judgment should we form of those who have devised images of God, or of the persons of the adorable Trinity?
items.e: We should adjudge their practice to be both unlawful and abominable.

items.h: Why unlawful?
items.e: Because directly contrary to the express letter of the law in this commandment, and many other scriptures, such as, Jer. 10:14, 15; Hos. 13:2, and particularly Deut. 4:15-19, 23 - "Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves, (for ye saw NO MANNER of similitude on the day that the Lord spake unto you in Horeb, out of the midst of the fire,) lest ye corrupt yourselves, and make you a graven image, the similitude of any figure, the likeness of male or female," &c.

items.h: How is it abominable?
items.e: As debasing the Creator of heaven and earth to the rank of his own creatures; and a practical denial of all his infinite perfections, Psalm 50:21.

items.h: May we not have a picture of Christ, who has a true body?
items.e: By no means; because, though he has a true body and a reasonable soul, John 1:14, yet his human nature subsists in his divine person, which no picture can represent, Psalm 45:2.

items.h: Why ought all pictures of Christ to be abominated by Christians?
items.e: Because they are downright lies, representing no more than the picture of a mere man: whereas, the true Christ is God-man; "Immanuel, God with us," 1 Tim. 3:16; Matt. 1:23.

items.h: Is it lawful to form any inward representation of God, or of Christ, upon our fancy, bearing a resemblance to any creature whatever?
items.e: By no means; because this is the very inlet to gross outward idolatry: for, when once the Heathens "became vain in their imaginations, they presently changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things," Rom. 1:21, 23.

items.h: What is it to worship God by images, according to the idolatrous practice of Papists?
items.e: It is either to make use of images, as pretended helps to devotion; or, to worship God before the images of saints, as intercessors with him.

items.h: Can any feigned image of God, or of Christ, be helpful in devotion?
items.e: No; it is the Spirit only who helpeth our infirmities in all acts of spiritual devotion, Rom. 8:26; and that faith which is necessary for acceptance in duty, fixes upon the word of the living God, as its sole foundation, and not upon dead images, Luke 16:31.

items.h: Will it excuse any from the charge of idolatry, that they pretend to worship the true God before images, or by them, as means of worship, and not the very images themselves?
items.e: Not at all; because this is a mean of worship expressly forbidden in this commandment, which prohibits all bowing down before images, upon whatever pretext it be - "Thou shalt not BOW DOWN thyself to them, nor serve them."

items.h: Do they worship images who bow down before them, even though it be the true God they intend to worship by them?
items.e: In scripture reckoning they do; Isaiah 2:8, 9 - "Their land is full of idols: they worship the work of their own hands. The mean man boweth down, and the great man humbleth himself."

items.h: Was it the ultimate intention of the Israelites in the wilderness to pay divine worship to the golden calf itself; or, to JEHOVAH, by it, and before it?
items.e: It was undoubtedly their ultimate intention to worship JEHOVAH, the true God, before that image; as appears from Ex. 32:5 - "When Aaron saw it, he built an altar BEFORE IT; - and said, "To-morrow is a feast to the Lord," (or JEHOVAH, as it is in the original.) And yet, because they did this, so directly contrary to the very letter of this commandment, they are charged with worshipping the image itself, verse 8:- "They have made them a golden calf, and have worshipped IT," &c.

items.h: Do not they who honour the picture of a prince, honour the prince himself?
items.e: If the prince forbid the making of his picture, it is a contempt of his authority to have it. God has strictly prohibited all images for religious purposes, and therefore it is impious to have or use them for these ends, Lev. 26:1, 30.

items.h: May images be worshipped at all, upon their own account?
items.e: No; because they are the work of man's hands: far inferior in dignity to man himself, Isaiah 45:9-18.

items.h: May they be worshipped on account of their ORIGINALS; or those whom they are designed to represent?
items.e: They may not; whether designed to represent God, or the saints.

items.h: Why may they not be worshipped as they are designed to represent God?
items.e: Because he never put his name in them; but declares his greatest hatred and detestation of them, Jer. 44:2-9.

items.h: Why may they not be worshipped as they are designed to represent eminent saints?
items.e: Because saints, however eminent, are only mere creatures; and therefore cannot be the objects of worship, either in themselves, or by their images, Acts 14:14, 15.

items.h: Can saints in heaven be intercessors for sinners on earth?
items.e: No; because intercession being founded on satisfaction, none but CHRIST can be the intercessor, as none but he is the propitiation for our sins, 1 John 2:1, 2.

items.h: Is it lawful, as some plead, to have images or pictures in churches, though not for worship, yet for instruction, and raising the affections?
items.e: No; because God has expressly prohibited not only the worshipping but the MAKING of any image whatever on a religious account; and the setting them up in churches, cannot but have a natural tendency to beget a sacred veneration for them; and therefore ought to be abstained from, as having at least an "appearance of evil," Isaiah 45:9-18. 1 Thess. 5:22.

items.h: May they not be placed in churches for beauty and ornament?
items.e: No; the proper ornament of churches is the sound preaching of the gospel, and the pure dispensation of the sacraments, and other ordinances of divine institution.

items.h: Were not the images of the cherubims placed in the tabernacle and temple, by the command of God himself?
items.e: Yes; but out of all hazard of any abuse, being placed in the holy of holies, where none of the people ever came: they were instituted by God himself, which images are not; and they belonged to the typical and ceremonial worship, which is now quite abolished.

items.h: Are our forefathers to be blamed for pulling down altars, images, and other monuments of idolatry, from places of public worship at the Reformation?
items.e: No; they had Scripture precept and warrant for what they did, Num. 33:52, and Deut. 7:5 - "Ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images, and cut down their groves, and burn their graven images with fire."

items.h: What do you understand by will-worship, the other leading sin forbidden in this command?
items.e: It is the worshipping God in any other way not appointed in his word.

items.h: Should there be an express appointment in the word for every part of divine worship in which we engage?
items.e: Undoubtedly there should; otherwise we are guilty of innovating upon the worship of God, and prescribing rules to the Almighty, which is both displeasing to him, and unprofitable to ourselves, Matt. 15:9.

items.h: Who are they that are guilty of innovating upon the worship of God?
items.e: All they who presumptuously annex their own superstitious inventions to the divine institutions, under pretence of their being teaching significant ceremonies; as they of the Popish and Episcopal persuasions do.

items.h: What are these significant ceremonies which they add to the instituted ordinances of God's worship?
items.e: The sign of the cross in baptism; kneeling at receiving the sacrament of the supper; erecting altars in churches; and bowing at the name of Jesus, are a few of many.

items.h: Why may not such ceremonies be used, when they are designed for exciting devotion, and beautifying the worship of God?
items.e: Because God has expressly forbidden the least addition to or abatement from the order and directions he himself has given in his word concerning his own worship, Deut. 12:30-32 - "What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not ADD thereunto, nor DIMINISH from it."

items.h: Were there not significant ceremonies in the Jewish worship, under the Old Testament?
items.e: Yes; but they were of express divine appointment; and by the same appointment abolished in the death and resurrection of Christ, Heb. 9:1-15.

items.h: May not significant ceremonies be founded on 1 Cor. 14:40 - "Let all things be done decently and in order?"
items.e: No; because that text speaks only of the decent and orderly observance of the ordinances of God already instituted, and not in the least of any thing new to be added as a part of worship.

items.h: Is reading of sermons or discourses from the pulpit an ordinance of God appointed in his word?
items.e: So far from it, that we find the contrary practised by our Lord while he was here upon earth, Luke 4:16, 23; where, after reading his text out of the prophet Esaias, it is said, he CLOSED the book, and "began to say unto them, This day is this Scripture fulfilled in your ears," &c.

items.h: How may we be further guilty of a breach of his commandment, than by idolatry and will-worship?
items.e: When we neglect, Heb. 10:25, contemn, Matt. 22:5, hinder, chap. 23:13, or oppose the worship and ordinances which God has appointed in his word, 1 Thess. 2:16; or tolerate those who publish and maintain erroneous opinions or practices, Rev. 2:14, 15, 20.

items.h: What is the doctrine of our Confession concerning the tolerating of those who publish and maintain erroneous opinions or practices?
items.e: Tha: "for their publishing of such opinions, or maintaining of such practices, as are contrary to the light of nature, or the known principles of Christianity, whether concerning faith, worship, or conversation, or to the power of godliness, they may lawfully be called to account, and proceeded against by the censures of the church, and by the power of the civil magistrates."67

items.h: What are the reasons annexed to the Second Commandment?
items.e: The reasons annexed to the Second Commandment, are, God's sovereignty over us, his propriety in us and the zeal he hath to his own worship.

items.h: Why does our Catechism make mention of REASONS ANNEXED to this and the three following commandments?
items.e: Because God himself has been pleased to subjoin to each of these precepts, the reasons, arguments, or motives, that should influence our obedience to them.

items.h: How many reasons are annexed to this Second Commandment?
items.e: THREE; contained in these words, "I the Lord thy God am a jealous God."

items.h: Which is the first of these reasons?
items.e: It is God's sovereignty over us, in these words I THE LORD; or, I JEHOVAH.

items.h: What do you understand by God's sovereignty over us?
items.e: It is his absolute supreme power, or right of dominion over us, as his creatures, Rom. 9:20, 21, by which he can dispose of, ver. 22, 23, and prescribe to us as seems to him good, Deut 6:17.

items.h: In what lies the strength of this first reason for worshipping God by means of his own appointment?
items.e: It lies in this, that being our sovereign Lord, it must be his sole prerogative to prescribe to us the means of his own worship; and, consequently, that it must be our duty to make his pleasure in this, both the rule and reason of our punctual observance of what he enjoins, Psalm 95:2, 3.

items.h: What is the SECOND reason annexed to this commandment?
items.e: It is his propriety in us, in these words, THY God.

items.h: What other propriety has God in us than by right of creation.
items.e: He has a propriety likewise by right of redemption, intimated in the preface to the commands, "I am the Lord THY God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage," Ex. 20:2.

items.h: Is it his propriety by right of creation, or by right of redemption, that constitutes the federal relation between him and us?
items.e: It is his propriety by right of redemption, Isaiah 43:1 - "I have REDEEMED thee; I have called thee by thy name: thou art MINE."

items.h: What influence should his propriety in us, as his people, have upon our receiving and observing the ordinances of his worship?
items.e: If we are his people: we are ransomed by the blood of his only begotten Son, and so under the strongest ties of duty and gratitude, to cleave to the precise manner of worship prescribed in his word, rejecting all other modes and forms whatever, Josh. 24:24.

items.h: What is the THIRD reason annexed to this commandment?
items.e: It is the zeal he hath to his own worship, in these words, - I AM A JEALOUS GOD.

items.h: In what sense is God said to be a jealous God?
items.e: Jealousy is ascribed to him (after the manner of men,) to denote that he puts no confidence in his creatures, Deut. 5:29 that he has his eye upon them; and is highly offended when they slight him and bestow that love upon any other, which is due to him alone, chap. 32:15-26.

items.h: What is it for God to have zeal for his own worship?
items.e: It is to have Such a regard for the ordinances of his own institution, as highly to resent or revenge any addition to, or alteration of them; of which there is an awful instance in Nadab and Abihu, who offered strange fire before the Lord, Lev. 10:1-4.

items.h: In what does God manifest his zeal for his worship?
items.e: Both by way of threatening, and by way of promise.

items.h: What does God threaten as a testimony of his zeal for his worship?
items.e: To visit "the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation of them that hate" him.

items.h: What is it to visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children?
items.e: It is to inflict punishment upon the children for the faults and offences of their fathers.

items.h: Are there any scripture examples of God's doing so?
items.e: As to temporal punishments there are: Seven of Saul's sons were hanged before the Lord, for his offence in slaying the Gibeonites, 2 Sam. 21:8, 9; and for the sins of Jeroboam, his whole house was utterly extinguished, 1 Kings 15:29, 30.

items.h: Is this thought just and equal among men?
items.e: Yes; as appears by the common practice of disinheriting the children of traitors and rebels for the treasonable practices of their fathers, in order to create a greater detestation of these crimes in others.

items.h: Whether are temporal judgments only, or spiritual and eternal plagues also, intended in this threatening?
items.e: Spiritual and eternal plagues are also intended, Matt. 25:41.

items.h: How does it appear that spiritual and eternal judgments are included in this threatening?
items.e: It appears from this, that the punishment threatened should bear some proportion to the mercy promised; so that if the mercy promised be of a spiritual and eternal nature, the judgments threatened must be of the same kind.

items.h: How does the scripture illustrate this?
items.e: By the issue of the final sentence at the great day, which is, that the wicked "go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into life eternal," Matt. 25:46.

items.h: How does it consist with the justice of God, to inflict spiritual and eternal judgments upon children for the sins of their parents?
items.e: It is entirely consistent with it; because the children punished with spiritual and eternal judgments, are only such as have shown themselves heirs to their fathers' sins, either by copying them, Jer. 31:29, 30, or not disapproving of and mourning for them; by which means their fathers' sins become their own, Psalm 49:13.

items.h: How can the visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children be reconciled with Ezek. 18:20 - "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.
items.e: This passage in Ezekiel is to be understood of the son who does not tread in the steps of his wicked father; as is evident from ver. 14, 17 - "If he beget a son that seeth all his father's sins, and doth not such like, he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live;" whereas the threatening in this commandment respects wicked children, who copy after the example of their graceless parents, as Nadab the son of Jeroboam did, who "walked in the way of his father, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to Sin" I Kings 15:26.

items.h: How does it appear from the threatening itself, that this is the meaning?
items.e: Because the children on whom God visits the iniquity of their fathers are expressly said to be "the third and fourth generation of them that HATE him."

items.h: Why does God threaten to visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation only, of them that hate him; and not to all succeeding generations of such children?
items.e: Not but that the haters of God to all generations shall meet with deserved punishment; but the threatening is limited to the third and fourth generation, for a greater judgment upon wicked parents, some of whom may live to see their posterity of these generations, and to read their own sin in the punishment of their offspring whom they have seduced; as Zedekiah, for his wickedness, saw his sons, and the princes of Judah, slain before his eyes, Jer. 52:3, 10.

items.h: What if such wicked parents should die, before they see their third and fourth generations?
items.e: In that case, if their consciences are not quite seared, they will die under the dread and fear of the judgments here threatened, befalling their children, Hos. 2:4; as well as of the fiery indignation which shall devour themselves, Heb. 10:27.

items.h: May not God sometimes visit the iniquities of the breakers of this commandment upon their godly children?
items.e: He will never visit the iniquities of the fathers upon their godly children with spiritual and eternal judgments, though sometimes he may do it with temporal calamities: as no doubt many pious Israelites were carried captive to Babylon for the sins of their fathers, Lam. 5:7; which, nevertheless, was for their real good, Jer. 24:5.

items.h: What may we learn from this threatening to visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children?
items.e: That as nothing can be more cruel than for parents to set a bad example before their children, Jer. 9:14, 15; so the example of forefathers will not vindicate their posterity in the way of sin, particularly in the practice of any corrupt or false worship, Ezek. 20:18, 21.

items.h: What is it, on the other hand, that God promises as an evidence of his zeal for his worship?
items.e: To show mercy to thousands of them that love him, and keep his commandments.

items.h: Who are they that truly love God?
items.e: They who, from a faith of his own operation, have complacency and delight in him as their own God and portion, Psalm 5:11.

items.h: What is it to keep his commandments?
items.e: It is to essay a uniform and self-denied obedience to the law as a rule, because Christ has fulfilled it as a covenant, Rom. 7:4.

items.h: What mercy does God show to them that love him, and keep his commandments?
items.e: He shows strengthening, Psalm 94:18, comforting, Psalm 31:7, directing, Ex. 15:13, and persevering mercy to them, 2 Sam. 7:15.

items.h: Does God show mercy to children because they are the offspring of godly parents?
items.e: No; but merely because so it pleases him, Rom, 9:15 - "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy."

items.h: What benefit then have the children of godly parents beyond others?
items.e: They have the privilege of a religious education, Gen. 18:19; are the children of many prayers, Job 1:5; and may plead the promise, "I WILL be a God to thee, and to thy seed after thee," Gen. 17:7.

items.h: Why does the threatening run only to the third and fourth generation of them that hate him, and yet the promise to thousands of them that love him?
items.e: To show that God has far greater pleasure in the exercise of mercy, than in the venting of wrath, Ezek. 33:11; and likewise for an encouragement, both to parents and children, to aim at "walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless," Luke 1:6.

items.h: Which is the Third Commandment?
items.e: The Third Commandment is, Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain: for the Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

items.h: What is required in the Third Commandment?
items.e: The Third Commandment requireth the holy and reverend use of God's names, titles, attributes, ordinances, word, and works.

items.h: What does this commandment require in general?
items.e: That the instituted means of God's worship be used in a right MANNER, becoming the majesty of him with whom we have to do, Psalm 5:7.

items.h: What is the duty directly opposite to the sin of taking God's name in vain?
items.e: It is the sanctifying of his name, Isaiah 8:13 - "Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself, and let him be your fear and your dread."

items.h: What do you understand by the NAME of God?
items.e: Every thing by which he is pleased to make himself known.

items.h: By what does God make himself known?
items.e: By his names, titles, attributes, ordinances, word, and works.

items.h: Does God need any name to distinguish him from all others?
items.e: No; because he is a most singular Being, quite well distinguished from all others, by the infinity and absolute perfection of his nature, Isaiah 44:6.

items.h: Why then are names ascribed to him in scripture?
items.e: That some knowledge of his nature and perfections may be conveyed to us, Acts 9:15.

items.h: What are the names by which he conveys the knowledge of himself to us?
items.e: He conveys the knowledge of his absolute, eternal, and immutable essence by the names of JEHOVAH, Ex. 6:3; JAH, Psalm 68:4; and, I AM, Ex. 3:14; the knowledge of his excellency and sovereignty, by the names GOD and LORD, Deut. 6:4; and the knowledge of the essential relation of the three divine persons among themselves, by the names of FATHER, SON, and HOLY GHOST, Matt. 28:19.

items.h: Is there any difference between God's names and his titles?
items.e: His names set forth what he is in himself; his titles, what he is to others.

items.h: How are God's titles commonly distinguished?
items.e: Into those that belong to him as the God of nature, and those which are ascribed to him as the God of grace.

items.h: What are the titles that belong to him as the God of nature?
items.e: They are such as these, The Creator of the ends of the earth, Isaiah 40:28; the Preserver of men, Job 7:20; King of nations, Jer. 10:7; and Lord of hosts, Isaiah 1:9.

items.h: What are the titles that are ascribed to him as the God of grace?
items.e: They are the following among others: The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Ex. 3:6; the Holy One of Israel, Isaiah 48:17; King of saints, Rev. 15:3; the Father of mercies, 2 Cor. 1:3; the hearer of prayer, Psalm 65:2; and the God of salvation, Psalm 68:20.

items.h: Which is the most common and ordinary title ascribed to God under the New Testament?
items.e: It is the infinitely amiable and encouraging title of "the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ," Eph. 1:3; 1 Pet. 1:3.

items.h: What comfortable views may we take of God, as he is the God and Father of our Lord. Jesus Christ?
items.e: In this light we may view him as a reconciled God, 2 Cor. 5:19; a pardoning and accepting God through Christ, Eph. 1:6, 7; and as our God and Father in him, John 20:17, - "I ascend unto my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God."

items.h: What is to be understood by God's attributes?
items.e: The perfections and excellencies which are ascribed to him as the essential properties of his nature.

items.h: What are God's ordinances?
items.e: The reading, preaching, and hearing of the word; the administration of the Sacraments; prayer and praise; religious fasting and thanksgiving.69

items.h: What are the ordinances in which the name of God is more immediately interposed?
items.e: The name of God is more immediately interposed in oaths, vows, and lots.

items.h: What is an OATH?
items.e: It is an act of religious worship, in which God is solemnly invoked, or called upon, as a witness for the Confirmation of some matter in doubt.

items.h: Why is it said to be an act of religious worship?
items.e: Because there is, or ought to be in every formal oath, a solemn invocation of the name of God, Deut. 6:13 - "Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God - and shalt swear by his name."

items.h: What is imported in calling upon God as a witness in an oath?
items.e: It imports, that we acknowledge him to be the infallible searcher of our hearts; the powerful avenger of all perjury and falsehood; and at the same time to be infinitely superior to us; "for men verily Swear by the greater," Heb. 6:16.

items.h: In what cases should an oath be required?
items.e: Only in cases that are doubtful, when the truth of things cannot be known with certainty any other way.

items.h: What is the end of an oath in a lawful judicature?
items.e: It is for confirmation of the truth formerly doubtful; and for terminating strife and contradiction among men. "An oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife," Heb. 6:16.

items.h: What are the necessary qualifications of a lawful oath?
items.e: That we swear - "in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness," Jer. 6:2.

items.h: What is it to swear in truth?
items.e: It is to take special care, that what is sworn be strictly agreeable to truth; and that there be an exact agreement between the sentiments of our minds, and the words of our mouth, without the least equivocation, or mental reservation.

items.h: What is it to equivocate, or dissemble in an oath?
items.e: It is to have an inward reserved meaning and sense of words, contrary to the common and ordinary acceptation of them, and that with a design to deceive.

items.h: In what consists the evil and sinfulness of this practice?
items.e: It destroys the nature and end of an oath, which is to bring forth nothing but the truth: it opens a wide door to all falsehood and lying, contrary to Eph. 4:25 - "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour;" and it unhinges the firmest bonds of society, that none can put confidence in another.

items.h: What is it to swear in judgment?
items.e: It is to swear with knowledge and deliberation; seriously pondering in our mind, what it is we are about to swear, and the solemn appeal we make to God in the oath, together with the dangerous risk we run, if we swear either falsely or ignorantly.

items.h: What is it to swear in righteousness?
items.e: It is to give our oath only in things lawful, or such as are consistent with piety towards God, and equity towards man; and likewise to give it on a lawful occasion.

items.h: When is a civil oath taken upon a lawful occasion?
items.e: When it is required by a lawful magistrate, for the ending of strife and debate, and the impartial administration of justice.

items.h: How do you prove that it is warrantable for Christians under the New Testament, to declare the truth upon oath, when called to it?
items.e: From this, that an oath, being no part of the ceremonial law, there can be no reason given why it was lawful to swear under the Old Testament, which will not apply in the like circumstances NOW; especially as there are approved examples of the use of an oath under the New Testament, 2 Cor. 1:23; Rev. 10:6; Heb. 6:16.

items.h: Does not our Lord say, Matt. 5:34, - "Swear not at all;" and the apostle James, chap. 5:12, "Above all things, swear not"?
items.e: These texts manifestly condemn profane swearing in ordinary conversation, and not lawful swearing in judgment, when called to do it; as appears from the injunction subjoined in both places, "Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay."

items.h: What is the ordinary outward form or sign, in scripture, of appealing to God in an oath?
items.e: It is the lifting up of the hand; as appears from Gen. 14:22; Dan. 12:7; Rev. 10:5, 6.

items.h: What are we to think of that mode of swearing, by touching and kissing the gospel?
items.e: It is evidently superstitious, if not idolatrous, and borrowed by the Papists from the heathens, who worshipped their idols in this manner, Job 31:27; Hos. 13:2.

items.h: How are oaths commonly distinguished as to their kinds?
items.e: Into assertory and promissory oaths.

items.h: What is an assertory oath?
items.e: It is an invoking God as a witness to the truth of what we declare about things past or present.

items.h: Why called assertory?
items.e: Because the party swearing, without any promise for the future, only asserts the things to have been, or to be at present, as he then swears.

items.h: What is the chief use of assertory oaths?
items.e: It is to determine suits and processes in human courts about matters of fact.

items.h: What is a promissory oath
items.e: It is the invoking God as a witness to the performance of a thing for the time to come, either absolutely or conditionally.

items.h: Why called promissory?
items.e: Because the party swearing promises or engages to do something hereafter.

items.h: What should be the subject matter of assertory oaths?
items.e: Such things as are both true and weighty, and which we know to be so.

items.h: What should be the subject matter of promissory oaths?
items.e: Such things as to our knowledge, are lawful, possible, and in our power to perform.

items.h: How may promissory oaths be subdivided?
items.e: Into civil and religious.

items.h: To what has a civil promissory oath a respect?
items.e: To :ontracts and engagements among men, whether of a more private or public nature.

items.h: May not the supreme magistrate require an allegiance of his subjects, or an oath of fidelity to obey his just and lawful commands?
items.e: It appears evidently from scripture that he may, Eccl. 8:2 - "I counsel thee to keep the king's commandment, and that in regard of the oath of God," 1 Chron. 29:24.

items.h: To what has a religious promissory oath a respect.
items.e: It respects the duties and services we owe more immediately to God, and the interests of religion.70

items.h: In what lies the obligation of an oath?
items.e: In the strong tie or bond that the party swearing comes under, to the performance of some duty engaged to.

items.h: How many fold is the obligation of a promissory oath?
items.e: TWOFOLD: one to the person to whom the oath is made, as a party; the other to God, by whom the oath is made, as a witness and avenger.

items.h: What is the difference between the obligation of a promise, and the obligation of an oath?
items.e: A man is bound to perform his promise as well as his oath: but an oath being an immediate invocation of the name of God as a witness and judge, it is, on this account, of a stronger obligation, and the breach of it a more heinous sin, than the breach of a simple promise.

items.h: Does not all obligation to duty respect a future time in which it is to be performed?
items.e: It necessarily does so, in the nature of the thing; although, in some cases, the time of performance may be very short after the obligation is contracted.

items.h: Under what obligation does a person come in an assertory oath, which respects the time past or present?
items.e: He comes under an obligation to declare the truth, and nothing but the truth, in what he is about to say; or, that his words shall exactly agree with his mind.

items.h: Under what obligation does a person come in a promissory oath, which respects the time to come?
items.e: He comes under an obligation to endeavour, as far as in him lies, to fulfil that which he has sworn; or, to perform all that he has promised by oath, Num. 30:2 - "If a man vow a vow unto the Lord, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth."

items.h: Is an oath about a thing lawful and possible obligatory, even though it be extorted by force or fear?
items.e: Undoubtedly it is: because of the reverence due to God, by whom the oath is made a witness and judge, Lev. 19:12 - "Ye shall not swear by my name falsely; neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the Lord."Matt. 5:33 - "Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths."

items.h: Is a person bound to pay such a sum to a robber as he has promised by his oath, for the ransom of his life?
items.e: He is certainly bound to pay it; because, of TWO PENAL evils, he voluntarily made choice of the least; to part with his money, rather than his life; accordingly, the righteous man, "sweareth to his OWN HURT, and changeth not," Psalm 15:4.

items.h: Is an oath, which is lawful as to the matter of it, though sinful as to the manner, and even obtained by, deceit, or rashly made binding and obligatory upon the person who has sworn it?
items.e: Yes; as is evident from the instance of the Gibeonites, who deceived Israel into a league with them by oath, and yet their oath was binding, Josh. 9:14-20.

items.h: Are oaths and contracts to be kept with Heathens and heretics?
items.e: No doubt they should, as well as with others. Zedekiah, king of Judah, was severely punished for his breach of oath to the king of Babylon, 2 Chron. 36:13; Ezek. 17:16. Besides, if infidelity and heresy do not nullify the marriage oath, neither ought they to make void any other lawful contract.

items.h: What is a vow?
items.e: It is a voluntary and deliberate engagement to God only as party, and that respecting matters of a sacred or religious character, Psalm 132:2-6.

items.h: What is the difference between an oath and a vow?
items.e: In an oath, man is generally the party, and God is brought in as the witness: but in a vow, God himself is always the sole party, besides his being a witness, Psalm 50:14. Isaiah 19:21.

items.h: What is the subject matter of vows?
items.e: Only things religious; or such as relate immediately to the glory of God, and the salvation of our souls.

items.h: How ought vows to be entered into?
items.e: In the exercise of faith; or, in the strength of the grace that is in Christ Jesus, John 15:5; without which there can be no performance, Phil. 4:13.

items.h: How many kinds of vows are there?
items.e: Two; personal and social.

items.h: What is a personal vow?
items.e: It is the act of an individual, or single person, taking hold of God's covenant of grace, or acquiescing in it as made with Christ, who is the all of it and thus engaging to be the Lord's, and to essay the practice of all duty in his strength. Is. 44:5 - "One shall say, I am the Lord's," Psalm 119:106 - "I have sworn, and will perform it, that I will keep thy righteous judgments."71

items.h: What is a social vow?
items.e: It is the joint concurrence of several individuals in the same exercise as in a personal one, openly avouching the Lord to be their God, Deut. 26:17; where Moses, speaking of all Israel, says, "Thou hast avouched the Lord this day to be thy God, to walk in his ways," &c.

items.h: When doth such a social vow commonly get the name of a NATIONAL COVENANT?
items.e: When the representatives of a nation, or the better part of them, concur in a covenant of duties, as ingrafted upon the covenant of grace, Jer. 50:4, 5 - "The children of Israel shall come, they and the children of Judah together, - saying, Come, and let us join ourselves to the Lord in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten." See also Neh. 9:33, and 10:1, 30.

items.h: How do you prove that national covenanting is a warrantable duty under the New Testament?
items.e: From its being promised in the Old Testament that this shall be a duty performed under the New, Isaiah 19:21 - "The Egyptians shall know the Lord in that day, and - they shall vow a vow unto the Lord, and shall perform it." Besides, if it was a moral duty upon special occasions, under the Old Testament (as appears from 2 Chron 15:12, and 34:31, 32; Neh. 9:38), it must remain to be the same, upon the like occasions, still; because Christ came not to destroy the law or the prophets, but to fulfil them, Matt 5:17.

items.h: Is our obligation to moral duties increased, by our vowing or engaging to perform them?
items.e: Although it is impossible that our obligation to moral duty can he increased by any deed of ours, beyond what it is already by the law of God, which is of the highest authority; yet by reason of our own voluntary and superadded engagement, this obligation from the law may make a deeper impression than before, Psalm 44:17, 18, and our sins receive a higher aggravation, if we either omit the duty engaged to, or commit the evil opposite to it, Deut. 23:21, 22.

items.h: What is a LOT, or lotting?
items.e: It is the laying aside the use of all means or second causes, and appealing directly to God, that he may, by his immediate providence, give a present decision respecting any matter in question "for the lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord," Proverbs 16:33.

items.h: Why are lots said to be an appeal to God?
items.e: Because, by casting of lots between two or more persons, or things, we, as it were, require him immediately to declare his mind by the event, which way the decision shall go, Acts 1:24, 26 - "Show whether of these two thou hast chosen. And the lot felt on Matthias."

items.h: In what cases may a decision be put upon the event of a lot?
items.e: Only in cases of great weight and absolute necessity, Josh. 7:13, 14.

items.h: Why should a lot be used only in cases of great weight and moment?
items.e: Because a lot being a material or implicit invoking of God to give a decision, it would be a wicked profanation of his name, to call him to determine in trifles, or things of little or no value.

items.h: Why should it be used only in cases of absolute necessity?
items.e: Because, where human prudence can determine, it would be a tempting of God, to require his decision.

items.h: What then is the end of lots?
items.e: It is the same as of oaths, to determine finally in momentous controversies, that which can be decided in no other way, Proverbs 18:18 - "The lot causeth contention to cease, and parteth between the mighty."

items.h: In what manner ought lots to be used?
items.e: In : most reverential manner, as in the presence of God, who pronounces the sentence; and in whose decision all parties ought cheerfully to acquiesce, Acts 1:24, 26 - "And they PRAYED - and gave forth their lots."

items.h: What is the word in which the name of God is declared?
items.e: The scriptures of the Old and New Testament.

items.h: What is meant by God's works in this answer?
items.e: His works of creation and providence; which last includes redemption.

items.h: What does this commandment REQUIRE, with reference to God's names, titles, attributes, ordinances, word, and works.
items.e: The holy and reverend use of them.

items.h: What is it to make a holy and reverend use of these?
items.e: It is, in all our meditations, speeches, and writings, to have the most profound respect and regard for every thing, by which God manifests his name and glory, Deut. 28:58.

items.h: When do we essay to make a reverend use of God's names, titles, and attributes?
items.e: When we view them as in Christ, and in this light draw virtue from them, for the increase of our faith and holiness, Ex. 23:21 - "Obey his voice - for my name is in him."

items.h: When do we endeavour a holy and reverend use of the ordinances?
items.e: When we view God as present in them, Matt. 28:20; and attend or perform them with a single eye to his glory, Psalm 86:9.

items.h: When do we use the word in a holy and reverend manner?
items.e: When we search and believe the scriptures, as testifying of Christ, John 5:39; and are directed by them as a lamp to our feet, and a light to our path, Psalm 119:105.

items.h: When do we essay to make a holy and reverend use of the works of God.
items.e: When we are enabled to make suitable improvement of the bright displays he has made of his glorious excellencies, in creation, providence, and redemption, so as to walk humbly and thankfully before him, Rev. 15:3, 4 - "Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints. Who shall not fear thee, O Lord! and glorify thy name for thou only art holy."

items.h: What is forbidden in the Third Commandment?
items.e: The Third Commandment forbiddeth all profaning or abusing of any thing whereby God maketh himself known.

items.h: What do you understand by profaning or abusing of any thing whereby God makes himself known?
items.e: It :s the using of his names, titles, attributes, ordinances, word, and works, in a rash, irreverent, and unbecoming manner.

items.h: How are God's names, titles, and attributes, profaned or abused by men?
items.e: Many ways: particularly, by blasphemy, perjury, sinful cursings, oaths, vows, and lots."72

items.h: :hat is blasphemy?
items.e: It is speaking in a reproachful, reviling, and under-valuing manner of God, Isaiah 36:20; of his word, Acts 13:45; or of any of his providential dispensations, Ezek. 18:25.

items.h: What is the aggravation of this sin?
items.e: It is an atheistical contempt of the most high God; - the greatest affront that can be done him by his creatures, Ex. 5:2.

items.h: May not persons be guilty of blasphemy in their hearts though never uttered in words?
items.e: Yes, undoubtedly they may; either when atheistical thoughts of him are harboured, Psalm 14:1; or, disparaging and unbecoming conceptions of him entertained, Psalm 10:11 and 50:21.

items.h: What was the punishment of blasphemy, at the hand of man, by the law of God?
items.e: It was death, Lev. 24:16 - "He that blasphemeth the name of the Lord, he shall surely be put to death."

items.h: What is perjury?
items.e: It is a breach or violation of any solemn oath or vow we have entered into or come under, Matt. 5:33 - "Thou shalt not forswear thyself."

items.h: When are persons guilty of perjury in assertory oaths?
items.e: When they assert such a thing, upon oath to be true, which yet they know to be false, like the witness against Naboth, 1 Kings 21:13; or even when they are doubtful and uncertain about the truth of what they are swearing; like the witnesses against Christ, whose witnessing did "not agree together," Mark 14:58, 59.

items.h: When are persons guilty of perjury in promissory oaths?
items.e: When they promise upon oath what they have no mind to perform; or when, without any insuperable impediment laid in their way, or any just and relevant excuse, they fail in the performance: as in the perjury of Zedekiah king of Judah, who broke his oath to the king of Babylon, Ezek. 17:16.

items.h: Is a person guilty of perjury, if he swears to do a thing impossible or unlawful?
items.e: Surely he is: for, if he swear to a thing impossible, he swears to a manifest lie; if he swear to do a thing unlawful, he is doubly perjured; both in making such an oath, and in fulfilling it, as was the case with Herod, Matt. 14:9, 10.

items.h: What is the aggravation of the sin of perjury?
items.e: It not only breaks all the bonds of society among men, but impeaches the omniscience of God himself, calling him to attest what conscience knows to be an untruth; and therefore God threatens, that his "curse shall enter into the house of him that sweareth falsely - and shall consume it, with the timber thereof, and the stones thereof," Zech. 5:3, 4.

items.h: How is God's name profaned by sinful cursings?
items.e: When God's wrath and vengeance are imprecated upon ourselves or others: or when the devil is in any manner invoked for harm.

items.h: For what do wicked persons wish, when they imprecate the wrath and vengeance of God upon themselves?
items.e: They do, in effect, pray, that God would hasten their everlasting destruction, and that their damnation may not slumber, but be speedily inflicted; 2 Pet. 2:3.

items.h: Do the devils themselves venture to wish for this?
items.e: No; they believe that there is farther wrath awaiting them at the judgment of the great day; and they tremble at the forethoughts of it, James 2:19; Jude verse 6.

items.h: What is the evil of imprecating divine vengeance upon others?
items.e: It is a piece of the most profane, presumptuous, and impudent freedom with the Majesty of heaven; as if he were bound to empty the vials of his wrath upon our fellow creatures, at our pleasure, and that in order to gratify our passionate revenge upon them, 2 Sam. 16:5, 8.

items.h: Is it not a most horrid and abominable wickedness to call or invoke the evil to TAKE ourselves or others?
items.e: Surely it is for it is a putting the devil in God's stead, or an employing of him to do God's work for him, even when he is delaying to do it himself; which is no less than devil-worship, and we ought not to "have fellowship with devils," 1 Cor. 10:20.

items.h: How is the name of God abused by sinful oaths?
items.e: When men take unlawful oaths that may be imposed upon them, and when, in their ordinary conversation, they swear by God, or by any thing by which he makes himself known; contrary to Matt. 5:37 - "Let your communications be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these, cometh of evil:" or of the evil one.

items.h: In what lies the heinousness of swearing in common discourse?
items.e: It is a most heaven-daring wickedness, even an insulting of the great God, our maker, to his face; a crime, which we dare not, without danger, be guilty of against our fellow creatures; and which is neither attended with the allurements of pleasure nor temptations of profit.

items.h: Is it a taking of God's name in vain, to swear by the creatures; such as, by heaven, by our life, soul, conscience, or the like?
items.e: Yes; because swearing by any of his creatures, is interpretatively a swearing by God the Creator and Preserver of all things, Matt. 23:22 - "He that sweareth by HEAVEN, sweareth by the throne of God, and by him that sitteth thereon."

items.h: Did not Joseph, who was a good man, swear repeatedly "by the life of Pharaoh"? Gen. 42:15, 16.
items.e: The goodness of the man did not excuse the sinfulness of the action: we are not to "do evil, that good may come," Rom. 3:8. For, though it may be alleged, that to say, "By the life of Pharaoh," is no more than to say, "As sure as Pharaoh lives;" yet the words themselves being in the form of an unlawful oath, which it would seem was commonly used by the Egyptians, they ought not, for this reason, to have been uttered.

items.h: Is swearing by faith, or troth, a formal profaning of God's name?
items.e: No doubt it is; for when a person swears in this manner, he tacitly invokes God to bear witness, that he is speaking faithfully and truly, and to punish him, if he is doing otherwise; which, in ordinary conversation, is undoubtedly sinful, and a falling "into condemnation," James 5:12.

items.h: Will a habit or custom of swearing in common discourse, be an excuse for it?
items.e: By no means; any more than a habit or custom of killing men, can be an excuse for wilful murder.

items.h: How is the name of God profaned by sinful vows?
items.e: Either when we solemnly enter into a resolution to do what is absolutely unlawful as Jezebel did, 1 Kings 19:2; or when we come under engagements to duty, and against sin, in our own strength, without a due dependence on the grace of God, as the greater part of the Israelites did, Deut. 5:27, 29; or, when we vow, and are not resolved to perform, as Johanan and his confederates did, Jer. 42:5, compared with verse 20.

items.h: When is the name of God profaned or abused by lots?
items.e: When God is appealed to by way of diversion, as in playing at cards, and dice, where the great God is most presumptuously invoked to determine who shall be the gainer. Lots are also unlawful, when there is an appeal by them to God in matters of small moment, which might be otherwise easily decided; this being too like the practice of the soldiers, who, after they had crucified Christ, did "cast lots for his vesture," John 19:23, 24.

items.h: How do men profane the name of God in their outward walk?
items.e: By making profession of religion in hypocrisy, and backsliding from it, Heb. 6:6; or, by committing such enormities and immoralities, as reflect dishonour upon it, and make the name of God to be evil spoken of, Rom, 2:24.

items.h: How are the ordinances of God profaned and abused?
items.e: Either when they are quite neglected, Acts 7:42, 43, or when they are attended in a formal, superficial, and customary manner, without seeking to meet with God in them, or to have spiritual food and nourishment to our souls by them, Isaiah 29:13, 14.

items.h: How is the word profaned and abused?
