items.e: Because God set a peculiar mark of his displeasure upon him, Gen. 4:15, (worse, in some sort, than natural death,) by protracting his miserable life, to be a fugitive, and a vagabond in the earth, and a visible monument of an intolerable load of guilt, and hopeless despair, ver. 11, 12.

items.h: What is the dismal effect of this sin upon murderers themselves, even though they escape capital punishment from men?
items.e: God frequently gives them up to the terror of a guilty conscience, which is their continual tormentor, Gen. 4:13, 14.

items.h: How has God testified his displeasure against this sin?
items.e: Ordinarily, by shortening the lives of murderers, Psalm 55:23 - "Bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days." And sometimes by transmitting temporal judgments to their posterity; as Saul's murder of the Gibeonites was punished in the death of seven of his sons, 2 Sam. 21:6, 8, 9.

items.h: How may murder be aggravated?
items.e: If committed under pretence of religion, as Jezebel murdered Naboth, 1 Kings 21:9, 10; and as the Papists perpetrate their massacres; or, if done under the disguise and mask of friendship, as Joab killed Amasa, 2 Sam. 20:9, 10; or, which is unspeakably worse, as Judas betrayed our Lord, Matt. 26:48, 49.

items.h: Does this command forbid only the taking away of our own life, and the life of our neighbour unjustly?
items.e: It forbids also whatsoever tends thereto.

items.h: What are those things which tend to the taking away of our own life?
items.e: "Neglecting or withdrawing the lawful and necessary means of preserving it: - all excessive passions, distracting cares, and immoderate use of meat, drink, labour, and recreation."92

items.h: How may we be guilty before God, of taking away the life of our neighbour, though we do not actually imbrue our hands in his blood?
items.e: We may be guilty this way in our hearts, with our tongues, and by our actions.

items.h: How may we be guilty of murder in our hearts?
items.e: By harbouring "sinful anger, hatred, envy, and a desire of revenge."93

items.h: May there be anger which is not sinful?
items.e: Yes; when there is a detestation of the sin, and yet no dislike of the person; in which sense the apostle says, "Be ye angry and sin not," Eph. 4:26.

items.h: What is the hazard of sinful anger?
items.e: "Whosoever is angry with his brother, without a cause, shall be in danger of the judgment," Matt. 5:22.

items.h: What is it to be in danger of the judgment?
items.e: It is to be in danger of eternal punishment in the other world, for the breach of this commandment, if rich and sovereign grace prevent it not, Proverbs 19:19.

items.h: How does hatred tend to take away the life of our neighbour?
items.e: It has such a tendency to it, that whosoever hateth his brother is accounted a murderer, 1 John 3:15.

items.h: What tendency has envy to the taking away of life?
items.e: As it is grieved at the good of another, or takes a secret pleasure in his death, Proverbs 27:4.

items.h: How does desire of revenge tend to take away life?
items.e: As it is accompanied with an inward habitual imprecation of some visible or remarkable judgment upon the person who is the object of it, quite contrary to the command of God, Rom. 12:19 - "Avenge not yourselves: - for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."

items.h: How may we be guilty of what tends to take away the life of our neighbour with our tongues?
items.e: By bitter and provoking words, Proverbs 12:18; or threatening, reviling and deriding speeches, Matt. 5:22.

items.h: How may we be guilty, this way, by our actions?
items.e: By oppression, Ezek. 18:18; quarrelling, Gal. 5:15; striking or wounding, Num. 35:21, and the like.

items.h: What may we learn from this commandment?
items.e: That however innocent we may be of the actual blood-shedding of others, yet we are still chargeable with the worst kind of murder, even that of our own souls, while we will not come to Christ, that we might have life, John 5:40, he being the only living and true way, chap. 14:6; and "no other name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved," Acts 4:12.

items.h: What is the Seventh Commandment?
items.e: The Seventh Commandment is, Thou shalt not commit adultery.

items.h: What is required in the Seventh Commandment?
items.e: The Seventh Commandment requireth the preservation of our own and our neighbour's chastity, in heart, speech, and behaviour.

items.h: What is chastity?
items.e: It is an abhorrence of all uncleanness, whether in the body, or in the mind and affections, Job 31:1.

items.h: What does this commandment require with reference to such chastity?
items.e: The preservation of it, both in ourselves, and in our neighbours.

items.h: What is the best means for preserving our own and our neighbour's chastity?
items.e: The cherishing in our minds and consciences a continual regard, reverence, and awe of the divine Majesty, and a fear of displeasing him, Proverbs 5:20, 21.

items.h: What influence will this have upon the preservation of chastity?
items.e: It will make us boldly resist all assaults or attacks that may be made upon it; as in the instance of Joseph, when solicited by his master's wife to lie with her, he refused; and said - "How can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" Gen. 39:7-9.

items.h: Wherein are we to preserve our own and our neighbour's chastity?
items.e: In heart, speech, and behaviour.

items.h: How ought we in heart to preserve our own chastity?
items.e: By resisting the very first emotions of lust in the soul, Proverbs 4:23; by repelling all wanton imaginations, Matt. 5:28; and by essaying both these in the way of praying to God that he would turn away our hearts and eyes from beholding vanity, Ps 119:37.

items.h: How ought we to preserve our neighbour's chastity in our hearts?
items.e: Not only by ardently desiring the preservation of it, but by loving one another with a pure heart fervently; 1 Pet. 1:22.

items.h: How ought we to preserve our own and our neighbours chastity in our speech?.
items.e: By "letting no corrupt communication proceed out of our mouth, but that which is good, to the use of edifying that it may minister grace unto the hearers," Eph. 4:29.

items.h: How should we do this in our behaviour?
items.e: By such a uniform modesty in our conduct and deportment, as may evidence that every one of us possesses his vessel, (that is, his body,) in sanctification and honour, 1 Thess. 4:4.

items.h: Why should we be so careful to preserve our chastity?
items.e: Because we should study to have our bodies to be the temples of the Holy Ghost, and therefore should keep them free from those pollutions which are so provoking to a holy God, 1 Cor. 6:19.

items.h: What is the ordinary mean of divine appointment for the preservation of chastity?
items.e: Lawful wedlock or marriage, 1 Cor. 7:2 - "Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband."

items.h: When was marriage first instituted?
items.e: Before the fall, in paradise, Gen. 2:24.

items.h: For what end was it instituted?
items.e: For the mutual help of husband and wife, Gen. 2:18; for the increase of mankind with a legitimate issue, and of the church with a holy seed, Mal. 2:15; and for preventing of uncleanness," 1 Cor. 7:2.94

items.h: What is necessary to constitute marriage?
items.e: The voluntary and mutual consent of both parties, Gen. 24:58, 67.

items.h: Who may be lawfully married?
items.e: "All sorts of people; who are able, with judgment, to give their consent," Heb. 13:4 - "Marriage is honourable in all."95

items.h: What is the duty of Christians with reference to marriage?
items.e: It is to marry "only in the Lord," 1 Cor. 7:39.

items.h: What is the native import of marrying "only in the Lord"?
items.e: It plainly imports, that "such as profess the true reformed religion should not marry with infidels, Papists, or other idolaters: neither should such as are godly be unequally yoked, by marrying with such as are notoriously wicked in their life, or maintain damnable heresies."96

items.h: What is an incestuous marriage?
items.e: It is that which is within the degrees of consanguinity, or affinity, forbidden in the word, Lev. 18:6-18.

items.h: What is the meaning of the words consanguinity and affinity?
items.e: CONSANGUINITY is a relation by blood, being between persons descended from the same family: AFFINITY is an alliance by marriage, between persons who were not blood relations before.

items.h: What is the general rule for preventing incestuous marriages?
items.e: The man may not marry any of his wife's kindred nearer in blood than he may of his own: nor the woman of her husband's kindred nearer in blood than of her own."97

items.h: Is it proper to call marriage a HOLY state?
items.e: No; because they who are without the visible church, such as Heathens, Turks, and Jews, may marry as well as the professed members of it; Heb. 13:4.

items.h: Was marriage instituted to signify the "mystical union that is between Christ and his church," as the Book of Common Prayer affirms?
items.e: No; because this borders too near upon making marriage a sacrament, as the Papists do; in as much as an outward visible sign, of divine institution, and a spiritual benefit signified by it, would make it partake of the nature of a sacrament.

items.h: Does not the apostle make it a significant sign, when he says, "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ loved the church?" Eph. 5:25.
items.e: He exhorts husbands to have such a love to their wives, as may bear a faint resemblance in some respects, to the love of Christ; but does not make the one a sign significant of the other.

items.h: Is not marriage called a great mystery? ver. 32.
items.e: It is not marriage that is called a great mystery, but the union that is between Christ and the members of his mystical body; as will appear by reading the whole verse, "This is a great mystery; but I speak concerning CHRIST and the CHURCH."

items.h: What is forbidden in the Seventh Commandment?
items.e: The Seventh Commandment forbiddeth all unchaste thoughts, words, and actions.

items.h: What is forbidden in this commandment under the name of ADULTERY?
items.e: All sorts of unchastity or uncleanness, of what kind, or in what manner soever committed, Eph. 5:3.

items.h: In what respects may persons be guilty of unchastity or uncleanness?
items.e: They may be guilty this way, in their thoughts, words, and actions.

items.h: When are persons chargeable before God with unchaste thoughts?
items.e: When lustful desires are entertained and gratified in the mind; and, as it were, acted in the imagination; Proverbs 6:18; Matt. 5:28.

items.h: What are the usual incentives to unchaste thoughts?
items.e: "Lascivious songs, books, pictures, dancings, stage-plays, and the like."98

items.h: What influence have stage-plays upon fomenting unchaste thoughts?
items.e: They are generally stuffed with such amorous adventures, many of them of a most criminal nature, that they have a native tendency to debauch and defile the mind. If "no corrupt communication" is to "proceed out of our mouth," according to Eph. 4:29; neither ought we to listen to it with our ears, as is done by those who attend the profane diversions of the stage.

items.h: What is meant by unchaste words?
items.e: All filthy, obscene, or smutty discourse; than which, nothing can be more grating and disagreeable to modest ears, Eph. 5:4.

items.h: What are the unchaste actions that are forbidden in this commandment?
items.e: Besides several others, that ought not to be named among Heathens, far less Christians, there are these following: polygamy, unjust divorce, fornication, and adultery, properly so called.

items.h: What is POLYGAMY?
items.e: It is the having more wives or husbands than one at the same time, Mal. 2:14.

items.h: Is this a sin contrary to the law of nature?
items.e: Yes; for it is contrary to the first institution of marriage; God having created but one woman, as a help meet for man; Gen. 2:22-25, compared with Matt. 19:5, 6.

items.h: Is it a sin prohibited in scripture?
items.e: Yes; Lev 18:18 - "Thou shalt not take a wife to her sister, to vex her - in her lifetime."

items.h: What is the meaning of taking a wife to her sister?
items.e: The meaning is, (according to the marginal reading,) Thou shalt not take one wife to another; that is, thou shalt not have more wives than one at a time.

items.h: But may not this be a prohibition of incest, namely, of marrying the wife's sister?.
items.e: No; because it is said, Thou shalt not do it in her lifetime; whereas it would be incestuous in a man to marry his sister-in-law after his wife's death, as well as to do it in her lifetime; so that the meaning is, Thou shalt not take another wife to her whom thou hast married, by which means they would become sisters.

items.h: Who was the first polygamist we read of in scripture?
items.e: Lamech, of the posterity of Cain, who had two wives, Gen. 4:19.

items.h: Were not several of the godly likewise guilty in this matter, as Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon, and others?
items.e: Yes; but though these and other bad actions of good men are recorded in scripture, they are not approved of, nor proposed for our imitation; but rather set up as beacons, to prevent our making shipwreck on the same rocks.

items.h: Has not God even testified his displeasure at the sin of polygamy, in the godly, though we do not read of his reproving them for it in express words?
items.e: Yes; he has testified his displeasure in the course of his providence, by the emulations, quarrels, and disturbances, that were thus occasioned in their families; as in the instances of Sarah and Hagar, in Abraham's family, Gen. 21:10, 11; of Leah and Rachel, in Jacob's, Gen. 30:1, 15; and of Hannah and Peninnah, in Elkanah's family, 1 Sam. 1:6.

items.h: Does not God seem to approve of polygamy, when he says to David, "I gave thee thy master's wives into thy bosom?" 2 Sam. 12:8.
items.e: It being the custom of those times, for succeeding kings to take possession of all that belonged to their predecessors, the meaning is, I have made thee king, in room of Saul, and have given thee the property of all that appertained to him: but we do not read of David taking any of Saul's wives into his bed.

items.h: What is an unjust DIVORCE?
items.e: It is the prosecuting and obtaining a dissolution of marriage, upon other grounds than such as are warranted in the word of God, and by right reason.

items.h: What are the grounds upon which a divorce may be sued for, and obtained, according to the word of God and right reason?
items.e: "Although the corruption of man be such as is apt to study arguments, unduly to put asunder those whom God hath joined together in marriage; yet nothing but adultery, or such wilful desertion, as can no way be remedied by the church, or civil magistrate, is cause sufficient of dissolving the bond of marriage, Matt. 19:8, 9; 1 Cor. 7:15."99

items.h: Did not Moses suffer the Israelites to put away their wives, upon slighter grounds than that of adultery as may be alleged from Deut. 24:1?
items.e: Moses, in the text cited, gives no positive command about divorces in such cases; but only, in order to restrain the licentious freedom of the Israelites, in turning off their wives, at their own hand, upon every trivial occasion, he enjoins that none put away his wife, but upon a legal process or a bill of divorce, obtained in the ordinary course of law; which is the true meaning of the place.

items.h: Why then does our Lord tell the Pharisees, Matt. 19:8, "Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, suffered you to put away your wives?"
items.e: The meaning is, Moses, because of the wicked and malicious disposition of the Jews, and in order to prevent a greater evil, namely, the ill usage, or even killing of their hated wives, (if they could not be separated from them) permitted processes of divorce to be legally commenced.

items.h: Why is it added, "but from the beginning it was not so?"
items.e: Because, according to the original institution of marriage, nothing could dissolve it but the death of one of the parties, Matt. 19:6 - "Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What, therefore, God hath joined together, let no man put asunder."

items.h: Is it lawful to marry after a divorce is obtained?
items.e: "It is lawful for the innocent party to sue out a divorce, and after the divorce, to marry another as if the offending party were dead."100

items.h: Is the innocent party obliged, from Matt. 5:32, to sue for a divorce?
items.e: No; divorces are not enjoined as a precept, but allowed as a privilege, which the innocent party may claim, or not, as they please.

items.h: What if the adultery be on both sides?
items.e: In that case the right of divorce seems to be taken away from each of them.

items.h: What is FORNICATION?
items.e: It is uncleanness committed between a man and a woman, both of them being unmarried; as it would seem Shechem and Dinah were, when guilty this way, Gen. 34:2.

items.h: Was this esteemed a sin among the Heathens?
items.e: No they made light of it, (as too many professed Christians have always done ) hence the synod of Jerusalem enjoined the converted Gentiles to "abstain from fornication," Acts 15:29.

items.h: In what lies the evil of this sin?
items.e: It defiles the body, 1 Cor. 6:18; stupefies the conscience, Hos. 4:11; and exposes to eternal wrath and damnation, 1 Cor. 6:9.

items.h: What is ADULTERY properly so called?
items.e: It is uncleanness committed between a man and a woman, either both or one of them at least, in a married relation.

items.h: What is it commonly called when both the guilty persons are married?
items.e: It is called double adultery, as was the case between David and Bathsheba, 2 Sam. 11:3, 4.

items.h: Whether are the consequences to families worse, when the man is married and the woman free; or when the woman is married and the man free?
items.e: The consequences to families seem to be worse when the woman is married; because a man's offspring is thus corrupted, and his inheritance is alienated to a spurious issue.

items.h: What are the aggravations of this heinous sin?
items.e: It is a breach of the marriage oath, Mal. 2:14; an involving of two at once in the same guilt, 1 Cor. 6:16; and is a crime committed after obtaining the remedy which God has provided against it, chap. 7:2.

items.h: What are the fatal effects of adultery in this life?
items.e: It consumes the body, Proverbs 5:11; wastes a man's estate, bringing him "to a piece of bread," chap. 6:26; and leaves an indelible blot upon his name: "His reproach shall not be wiped away," ver. 33.

items.h: What will be the effect of it in the life to come?
items.e: Eternal wrath and damnation, if rich mercy and grace prevent it not, Eph. 5:5.

items.h: How does God testify his abhorrence of this sin?
items.e: By declaring that he will reserve the punishment of it, in his own hand, to be inflicted in a very peculiar manner, upon such as are guilty of it, Heb. 13:4 - "Whore-mongers and adulterers God will judge."

items.h: What are the usual incentives to this and other acts of uncleanness?
items.e: Drunkenness, Gen. 19:33; "fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness," Ezek. 16:49.

items.h: What is the evil of idleness?
items.e: It is a deliberate wasting of precious time, to the manifest detriment both of soul and body, Eccl. 10:18; and is a fit season for temptations to lust, Proverbs 7:7, 8.

items.h: In what consists the evil of gluttony?
items.e: It indisposes for all duty, both religious and civil, Proverbs 23:21; and is making a god of our belly, Phil. 3:19.

items.h: What is the evil of drunkenness?
items.e: It deforms the image of God in the soul, by divesting a man of the right use of his reason; and leaves him defenceless against all temptations, Proverbs 23:29, 30.

items.h: What are the proper remedies against lust, and all the incentives to it?
items.e: A serious reflection upon the all-seeing eye of an infinitely holy God, Gen. 39:9; walking "in the Spirit," which will preserve us from fulfilling "the lusts of the flesh," Gal. 5:16; keeping a strict watch over our hearts, Proverbs 4:23; studying to shun all occasions of this sin by the external senses, Job 31:1; and fervent prayer to God to be kept from it, and all temptations to it, Psalm 119:37.

items.h: Which is the Eighth Commandment?
items.e: The Eighth Commandment is Thou shalt not steal.

items.h: What is required in the Eighth Commandment?
items.e: The Eighth Commandment requireth the lawful procuring and furthering the wealth and outward estate of ourselves and others.

items.h: What is the subject matter of this commandment?
items.e: The wealth and outward estate of ourselves and others.

items.h: What does it require with reference to these?
items.e: The procuring and furthering of them.

items.h: In what manner does it enjoin us to procure and further them?
items.e: Only in a lawful manner; for it requires the LAWFUL procuring and furthering of them.

items.h: Whose wealth is it we should procure and further?
items.e: Our own wealth, and that of others.

items.h: By what lawful means should we procure and further OUR OWN wealth?
items.e: By labour and industry in some honest calling, Eph. 4:28.

items.h: What is included in the labour and industry we should exercise in our respective stations and callings?
items.e: Frugality in managing the affairs of our calling, and a moderate endeavour to recover our own when wrongfully detained from us.

items.h: What is to be understood by frugality in managing the affairs of our calling?
items.e: Prudence and moderation in our expenses, so as to be sure always to spend within our incomes, Proverbs 31:16.

items.h: Is it warrantable to go to law, for recovering our own, when wrongfully detained?
items.e: Yes, surely; provided other means have been previously tried without success.

items.h: How do you prove that it is warrantable for Christians to go to law with one another, when urged by necessity?
items.e: From the lawfulness of magistracy, which is the ordinance of God, Rom. 13:2, "for the punishment of evil doers, and for the praise of them that do well," 1 Pet. 2:14.

items.h: Does not our Lord find fault with this method, when he says, "If any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also?" Matt. 5:40.
items.e: The meaning is, that we should rather part with a little of our right, than run ourselves into unnecessary charges at law, perhaps vastly beyond the value of what we are seeking to regain; and thus discover a contentious and quarrelsome spirit, unbecoming Christianity.

items.h: Does not the apostle also blame Christians for this practice, when he says, "Ye go to law one with another; why do ye not rather take wrong?" 1 Cor. 6:7.
items.e: The apostle is there speaking of bringing pleas unnecessarily before Heathen magistrates; and his meaning is, that Christians should make up differences among themselves, by submitting to arbitration; or even by suffering some wrong, rather than by vexatious law-suits, (especially about lesser matters) thus bringing a scandal upon the religion which they profess.

items.h: How is the necessity of labouring in an honest calling enforced in scripture?
items.e: From the necessity of eating: the apostle argues from the natural necessity of the one, to the moral necessity of the other, 2 Thess. 3:10 - "This we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

items.h: Can we procure and further our wealth and outward estate, merely by our own labour and industry?
items.e: Our own industry is necessary; but without the Lord's blessing upon it, it will not be successful; "for it is the blessing of the Lord that maketh rich," Proverbs 10:22.

items.h: What ends should we propose to ourselves, in endeavouring to further, or increase, our own outward estate?
items.e: That we may honour the Lord, with our substance, Proverbs 3:9; live comfortably ourselves, Eccl. 5:19; and be useful to others, Eph. 4:28.

items.h: By what means should we procure and further the wealth and outward estate of OTHERS?
items.e: By exercising justice and righteousness towards all, Psalm 15:2; and by relieving the wants and necessities of those who stand in need of our charity, 1 John 3:17.

items.h: What is the rule and standard of that justice and righteousness we should exercise towards all men?
items.e: That we so deal with others, as we would have them deal with us, if we were in their place or condition; or, that we should never do that to another, which, if we were in the other's place or circumstances, we would reckon to be unjust, Matt. 7:12.

items.h: In what cases is this rule to be particularly applied, according to the scope of this commandment?
items.e: In all contracts, or matters of traffic and commerce between man and man; and likewise in making satisfaction for injuries.

items.h: How is it to be applied in contracts, or matters of traffic between man and man?
items.e: It is to be applied thus: that in buying and selling, there be always a just proportion between the price and the thing sold; or, that the sale be according to the worth or value of the goods; without taking the advantage of ignorance or poverty on either side, Gen. 23:15, 16.

items.h: How may the worth and value of goods be known?
items.e: By this general maxim, That every thing is worth as much as it may be currently sold for.

items.h: May not the price of the same commodity vary and change at different times?
items.e: Yes; according to the plenty or scarcity of the commodity at the time of sale.

items.h: What satisfaction should be made to others, for taking or detaining what belongs to them, or in any manner defrauding them?
items.e: No other satisfaction is agreeable to God's will of precept, or will gain the approbation of men, but RESTITUTION, if the injuring party is ever capable to make it, Lev. 6:2-6; 1 Sam. 12:3.

items.h: What if the person to whom the restitution should be made, or his nearest of kin, cannot be found?
items.e: In that case, what has been unjustly detained ought to be given to the poor, or some pious use, Num. 5:8.

items.h: Is relieving the necessities of the poor a duty required in this commandment?
items.e: Yes; because it is a furthering the outward estate of our neighbour who is in want.

items.h: Why should we relieve the necessities of the poor?
items.e: Because, "He that hath pity upon the poor, lendeth to the Lord; and that which he hath given, will he pay him again," Proverbs 19:17.

items.h: Who are the proper objects of Charity?
items.e: All who are in real poverty and want, and are not able to work; especially those "who are of the household of faith," Gal. 6:10.

items.h: How should our acts of charity be managed?
items.e: They should be conducted with prudence, namely, as our own circumstances will permit, and the necessity of the object requires, 1 John 3:17.

items.h: When should we perform acts of charity?
items.e: Presently, if the necessities of those whom we are bound to relieve, call for present assistance, Proverbs 3:28.

items.h: What should we shun or avoid, in our acts of charity?
items.e: All ostentation, or a desire to be seen of men, and commended by them, Matt. 6:2-5.

items.h: What is forbidden in the Eighth Commandment?
items.e: The Eighth Commandment forbiddeth whatsoever doth or may unjustly hinder our own or our neighbour's wealth or outward estate.

items.h: What does the forbidding of THEFT necessarily suppose?
items.e: That there are distinct rights and properties among men, which cannot be justly invaded or encroached upon, Lev. 6:4.

items.h: What would be the necessary consequences of a community of goods among men?
items.e: It would destroy traffic and commerce; abolish all acts of charity; encourage sloth and idleness; and if there were no right and property there could be no encroachment upon it by theft or stealing.

items.h: From whom are we forbidden to steal?
items.e: Both from ourselves and others.

items.h: How may we be said to steal from OURSELVES?
items.e: By idleness, niggardliness, and prodigality.

items.h: How do we steal from ourselves, or impair our own estates, by idleness?
items.e: When we either live without a lawful calling, Proverbs 19:15; or neglect it, if we have any, chap. 18:9.

items.h: How may a person be said to steal from himself by niggardliness?
items.e: When he defrauds himself of the due use and comfort of that estate which God has given him, Eccl. 6:2.

items.h: How do persons on the other hand, steal from themselves, by prodigality?
items.e: By being lavish and profuse in spending above their income, Proverbs 23:20, 21.

items.h: What is the sin which is more directly pointed at in this commandment?
items.e: It is stealing from OTHERS; or laying hands upon, and taking away unjustly, that which is the right and property of another.

items.h: How many ways may persons be said to steal from others, or unjustly hinder their neighbour's wealth or outward estate?
items.e: Several ways; particularly, by theft, robbery, resetting, defrauding, monopolising, and taking unlawful usury.

items.h: What is theft?
items.e: It is the taking away clandestinely, or privily from another, that which is his, Lev. 19:11.

items.h: How is theft commonly distinguished?
items.e: Into private and public.

items.h: What is private theft?
items.e: It is the taking away less or more of any private person's property, without their knowledge or consent, Obadiah ver. 5.

items.h: Against whom is public theft committed?
items.e: Both against the church and commonwealth.

items.h: How is public theft called, as committed against the church?
items.e: Either Simony or sacrilege.

items.h: What is Simony?
items.e: It is the buying and selling of ecclesiastical places and offices for money, or other good deeds; so called, from the wicked practice of Simon Magus, who offered the apostles "money, saying, Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost," Acts 8:18, 19.

items.h: What is sacrilege?
items.e: It is the taking away or alienating of any thing which has been dedicated to a sacred use, Proverbs 20:25; Mal. 3:8.

items.h: Why are these called public theft, when, for the most part, they are privately committed?
items.e: Because they very much affect the public interest and welfare of the church; nothing having a greater tendency to her ruin, than Simoniacal compacts and sacrilegious usurpations.

items.h: In what consists public theft, as committed against the commonwealth?
items.e: In embezzling the current coin, or doing detriment to the public for private advantage, Rom. 13:7; Phil. 2:4.

items.h: What is robbery or rapine?
items.e: It is the taking away the goods of another by violence and open force, Job 20:19.

items.h: In what lies the aggravation of this crime?
items.e: In its being an avowed pillaging or plundering of our neighbour; and in being ordinarily accompanied with a threatening to take away his life, if he ventures to make the least resistance, Judges 9:25.

items.h: What is the evil of resetting101, or receiving of what is taken away, whether by stealth or violence?
items.e: It is a manifest encouragement of, and participation with thieves and robbers in their sins, Psalm 50:18; and consequently, a coming under the same guilt and condemnation with them, Proverbs 29:24.

items.h: How do men commonly defraud one another?
items.e: In buying, selling and borrowing.

items.h: How do they defraud in buying?
items.e: By depreciating and vilifying what they intend to buy, that they may have it cheaper than the value, Proverbs 20:14.

items.h: How do they defraud one another in selling?
items.e: By taking an unreasonable price, 1 Thess. 4:6; or, cheating by false weights and measures, Deut. 25:13-15.

items.h: How do they defraud in borrowing?
items.e: When they borrow what they know they can never be able, in the ordinary course of providence, to pay, Psalm 37:21.

items.h: If a man's creditors compound with him for less than he owes, is he therefore discharged of the whole debt?
items.e: Though his creditors, for fear of losing all, may compound and discharge for a part, so that there can be no action in law for the remainder; yet, in the court of conscience, and before God, he is bound, if ever he is able, to pay every farthing: and, if he is an honest man, he will never reckon his substance his own, till he do it, Rom. 13:8.

items.h: How may servants defraud their masters?
items.e: By wasting their masters' goods, which they may have in their hands; and not working faithfully for their wages, Titus 2:9, 10.

items.h: How may masters defraud their servants?
items.e: By detaining from, or tricking them out of their wages, Lev. 19:13; or by exacting of them too rigorous labour, Ex. 5:9.

items.h: What is it to monopolise?
items.e: It is to engross commodities, in order to enhance the price of them.

items.h: What is the worst kind of monopolising or forestalling?
items.e: It is the buying up grain, or other provisions, in large quantities, in order to exact a higher price for them afterwards.

items.h: In what consists the evil of this sin?
items.e: They who are guilty of it enrich themselves upon the spoils of others, Ezek. 22:29; they "grind the faces of the poor," Isaiah 3:15; and bring upon themselves the curse of the people, Proverbs 11:26 - "He that withholdeth corn, the people shall CURSE him; but blessings shall be upon the head of him that selleth it."

items.h: What is it to take USURY, according to the proper signification of the word?
items.e: It is to take gain, profit, or interest, for the loan of money.

items.h: What kind of usury or interest is lawful?
items.e: That which is moderate, easy, and no way oppressive, Deut. 23:20, compared with Ex. 22:21.

items.h: How do you prove that moderate usury is lawful?
items.e: From the very light of nature, which teaches, that since the borrower proposes to gain by the loan, the lender should have a reasonable share of his profit, as a recompense for the use of his money, which he might otherwise have disposed of to his own advantage, 2 Cor. 8:13.

items.h: What is the usury condemned in scripture, and by right reason?
items.e: It is the exacting of more interest or gain for the loan of money, than is settled by universal consent, and the laws of the land, Proverbs 28:8 - "He that by usury, and unjust gain, increaseth his substance, shall gather it for him that will pity the poor."

items.h: How do you prove from scripture, that moderate usury, or common interest, is not oppression in itself?
items.e: From the express command laid upon the Israelites not to "oppress a stranger," Ex. 23:9; and yet their being allowed to take usury from him, Deut. 23:20; which they would not have been permitted to do, if there had been an intrinsic evil in the thing itself.

items.h: Is it warrantable to take interest from the poor?
items.e: By no means; for, if such as are honest, and in needy circumstances, borrow a small sum towards a livelihood, and repay it in due time, it is all that can be expected of them; and therefore the demanding of any profit or interest, or even taking any of their necessaries of life in pledge, for the sum, seems to be plainly contrary to the law of charity, Ex. 22:25-28; Psalm 15:5.

items.h: Were not the Israelites forbidden to take usury from their brethren, whether poor or rich? Deut. 23:19 - "Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother."
items.e: This text is to be restricted to their poor brethren, as it is explained, Ex. 22:25, and Lev. 25:25, 35; or, if it respects the Israelites indifferently, then it is one of the judicial laws peculiar to that people, and of no binding force now.

items.h: What is the spring of all these different ways by which men defraud and injure one another in their outward estate?
items.e: Covetousness, Luke 12:15, or an inordinate prizing and loving of worldly goods, Psalm 62:10.

items.h: What should affright and deter every one from such wicked practices?
items.e: The consideration of the curse that shall enter into the house of the thief, Zech. 5:3, 4; and of the vengeance that shall light upon such as go beyond and defraud their neighbour: for, "the Lord is the avenger of all such," 1 Thess. 4:6.

items.h: Which is the Ninth Commandment?
items.e: The Ninth Commandment is, Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.

items.h: What is required in the Ninth Commandment?
items.e: The Ninth Commandment requireth the maintaining and promoting of truth between man and man, and of our own and our neighbour's good name, especially in witness-bearing.

items.h: In what does the Ninth Commandment differ from the three preceding ones?
items.e: The three commands immediately preceding, have a respect to the injuries that may be done to ourselves or others by deeds or actions; but the ninth has a reference to wrongs done by words.

items.h: What is the general duty required in this commandment?
items.e: It is the maintaining and promoting of truth between man and man.

items.h: What is the TRUTH, between man and man, we are required to maintain and promote?
items.e: It is the strict veracity of our words or speeches, in whatever we assert or deny; whether in our ordinary conversation, or in our oaths, promises, bargains, and contracts, Zech. 8:16 - "Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour."

items.h: In what consists the strict veracity that ought to be in our words and speeches?
items.e: In uttering things as they really are in themselves, according to our belief of them; that is, that there be an exact agreement and harmony between our thoughts, words, and the things themselves, Psalm 15:1, 2 - "Who shall dwell in thy holy hill? He that - speaketh truth is his heart."

items.h: Why will God have nothing to be uttered but strict truth?
items.e: Because he is "a God of truth, and without iniquity; just and right is he," Deut. 32:4.

items.h: Is it lawful at any time to conceal part of the truth?
items.e: Yes; when neither the glory of God, nor our own, or our neighbour's good requires that the whole of it be told; only no untruth must be uttered in concealing it, 1 Sam. 16:2, 5.

items.h: What is the chief end for which the tongue or gift of speech is conferred upon us?
items.e: That we may thus glorify God by praying to, Psalm 50:15, and praising him, verse 23; and by contending earnestly for, Jude verse 3, and confessing his truth, Rom. 10:10; hence is the tongue called our glory, Psalm 30:12 - "To the end that my GLORY (that is, my tongue, as on the margin) may sing praise unto thee, and not be silent."

items.h: What is the subordinate end of it?
items.e: The edification and profit of our fellow-creatures, Eph. 4:29 - "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good, to the use of edifying;" (margin, "to edify profitably,") in opposition to the insipid and vain talk which is in the mouths of most men.

items.h: What is the particular duty required in the Ninth Commandment?
items.e: That we maintain and promote our own and our neighbour's good name, especially in witness-bearing.

items.h: What is a good name?
items.e: It is the having of reputation and esteem, especially among the sober and religious, Psalm 16:3, and 101:6.

items.h: How may a good name be obtained?
items.e: By being useful in the world, in the several stations and relations in which adorable providence has placed us, Psalm 112:9.

items.h: Is self-commendation a fit mean to obtain a good name?
items.e: No; it is ordinarily the highway to procure scorn and contempt, 2 Cor. 10:12.

items.h: Does not the apostle commend himself, when he says, "In nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles?" 2 Cor. 12:11.
items.e: He only magnifies and exalts his office, and at the same time lessens and disparages himself; for, although he says, "In nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles," yet he immediately subjoins, "though I be nothing;" and 1 Cor. 15:9 - "I am the least of the apostles, who am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God."

items.h: May we not commend the grace of God in us?
items.e: To be sure we may; for, whatever is spoken to the commendation of free grace, is for the abasement of self, 1 Cor. 15:10 - "By the grace of God I am what I am."

items.h: How ought we to maintain and promote our own good name?
items.e: Not only by a blameless walk and conversation before the world, Phil, 2:15; but likewise by vindicating ourselves from the calumnies and aspersions that may be injuriously cast upon us, Acts 24:12, 13.

items.h: With what frame of spirit ought the lawful vindication of ourselves to be managed?
items.e: With moderation, meekness, and readiness to forgive those who have reproached and injured us, Col. 3:12, 13.

items.h: Who ought, in a special manner, to maintain and promote their own good name?
items.e: This is especially incumbent on professors of religion, Matt. 5:16; and such as are in places of public trust, Titus 2:7, 8.

items.h: Why should professors be careful to maintain their good name?
items.e: Because the loss of it tends to reflect dishonour on religion, by which the enemies of it take occasion to blaspheme, 2 Sam. 12:14.

items.h: What is the advantage of a good name?
items.e: A good name procures mutual love to, and confidence in one another; and, consequently, tends to promote the interests both of sacred and civil society; on which account "a good name" is said to be "better than precious ointment," Eccl. 7:1; and "rather to be chosen than great riches," Proverbs 22:1.

items.h: What does this command require in reference to our neighbour's good name?
items.e: The maintaining and promoting it, "as we would do our own," Phil. 2:4; and that both in his presence and in his absence.

items.h: How should we behave in the presence of our neighbour, for maintaining and promoting of his good name?
items.e: When we observe any thing faulty in him, which deserves present notice, we should reprove it with meekness and love, Lev. 19:17; and what is really commendable we should prudently encourage and applaud, Rom. 1:8.

items.h: How should we maintain and promote the good name of others in their absence?
items.e: By commending what is praise-worthy in them, 3 John ver. 12; vindicating their character when unjustly attacked, Proverbs 25:23; and by covering their infirmities and blemishes, so far as can be done in a consistency with truth, and the credit of religion, 1 Pet. 4:8.

items.h: Why is the word ESPECIALLY subjoined to witness-bearing?
items.e: Because, as we should give testimony to truth on all occasions, so, in a special manner, when called by lawful authority to declare the matter of fact upon oath, Jer. 4:2.

items.h: What special obligation lies upon us, to declare the true matter of fact, between man and man, when called to do it upon oath?
items.e: In an oath, God is appealed to, that we will declare nothing but the truth, as we shall answer to him at the great day; and therefore, our doing otherwise, either out of hatred, or favour, is laying ourselves open to his immediate wrath and displeasure, according to Mal. 3:5 - "I will be a swift witness - against false swearers, - saith the Lord of hosts."

items.h: What is forbidden in the Ninth Commandment?
items.e: The Ninth Commandment forbiddeth whatsoever is prejudicial to truth, or injurious to our own or our neighbour's good name.

items.h: What does this command forbid in general?
items.e: Whatsoever is prejudicial to truth.

items.h: What are we to understand, by that which is prejudicial to truth?
items.e: All falsehood and lying of whatever kind, James 3:14 - "Lie not against the truth."

items.h: What is the formal nature and meaning of a LIE?
items.e: It is voluntarily to speak or express what we know to be false, as the old prophet at Bethel did to the man of God, 1 Kings 13:18.

items.h: How is a lie aggravated?
items.e: When it is uttered with a design to deceive, and to harm others by it; like the devil, when he said, "Ye shall not surely die. - Ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil," Gen. 3:4, 5.

items.h: May not persons utter what is untrue or false and yet not be guilty of a lie?
items.e: Yes; and that either through ignorance or misinformation.

items.h: When may they be said to utter what is false through ignorance, and yet not be guilty of lying?
items.e: When they speak rashly, according to their present conception of things, without due examination; as the barbarians, when they "saw the venomous beast hang on Paul's hand, said: among themselves, No doubt this man is a murderer," &c., Acts 28:4.

items.h: When may we utter what is false through misinformation, and not be guilty of a lie?
items.e: When we speak according to the report we have had from others, without any suspicion of being imposed upon; as Jacob did, when, by the imposition of his sons, (who had sold Joseph into Egypt, and dipped his coat in he blood of a kid) he said, "It is my son's coat; an evil beast, hath devoured him: Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces," Gen. 37:33.

items.h: How many sorts of lies are there?
items.e: They are commonly ranked into three sorts; namely, ludicrous, pernicious, and officious lies.

items.h: What is a ludicrous or jocose lie?
items.e: It is when persons relate things they know to be false, with a design to make a jest or diversion to others.

items.h: What is it to be guilty of a pernicious lied?
items.e: It is to contrive or spread some malicious report we know or suspect to be false, on purpose to bring about some hurt or damage to another, as Ziba did against Mephibosheth, 2 Sam. 16:3.

items.h: What is the aggravation of a pernicious lie?
items.e: It is the very worst sort of lying, being both a contempt of the omniscient God, who is witness to the falsehood; and a deliberate intention to do injury to our neighbour, though in our conscience we believe him innocent of what we lay to his charge.

items.h: What is it for a person to make an officious lie?
items.e: It is to tell a downright untruth, for their own, or their neighbour's safety and security in time of danger, as Rahab did who hid the spies in the roof of her house, and yet alleged they were gone out of the city, and that she knew not where they went, Josh. 2:4-6.

items.h: Does not the apostle ascribe this action of hers to her faith, when he says, Heb. 11:31 - "By faith, Rahab, the harlot, perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace?"
items.e: No; What he ascribes to her faith is, her having received the spies with peace, that is, her having consulted their safety and preservation with the greatest care and diligence; but not the lie she invented in order to conceal them. Her protecting the spies is commended, but not the manner in which she did it.

items.h: Who are they that plead in favour of officious lies?
items.e: The Papists, Socinians, and most of our modern moralists.

items.h: What arguments do they allege in defence of this sort of lying?
items.e: That it has been practised by saints in scripture; and that it is so far from being hurtful to any, that it has been beneficial to some in certain cases.

items.h: What answer is to be given to the practice of the saints in this matter?
items.e: That their sinful failures, in this and other instances, are not recorded in scripture for imitation, but for caution and warning, that we fall not into the same snares.

items.h: How do you answer the other argument for officious lying, "That it is so far from being hurtful to any, that it has been beneficial and advantageous to some, in certain cases, particularly in saving the life of a dear friend, or useful member of society, which might otherwise have been manifestly endangered?"
items.e: It is answered thus, that in no case are we to do evil that good may come, Rom. 3:8. If we are not to speak wickedly for God, nor talk deceitfully for him, according to Job 13:7, neither are we to do so, though it were for the benefit of all mankind, or the best among them.

items.h: How do you prove lying to be sinful, or unlawful, in itself?
items.e: From this, that lying of all sorts, without exception, is condemned in scripture, as hateful and abominable to God, Proverbs 6:17, 19, and 12:22; Col. 3:9.

items.h: Who is the author and father of lies?
items.e: The devil, John 8:44 - "When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own; for he is a liar, and the father of it."

items.h: How does God testify his displeasure against lying of all kinds?
items.e: By declaring that "he who speaketh lies shall perish," Proverbs 19:9; accordingly it is said, "ALL liars shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone," Rev. 21:8.

items.h: What is more particularly forbidden in this commandment, according to the answer?
items.e: Whatever is injurious to our own or our neighbour's good name.

items.h: How may we injure our own good name?
items.e: By a vain-glorious commendation of ourselves, 2 Tim 3:2; by despising of others who ought justly to be esteemed, Luke 18:9, 11; or by doing any thing scandalous and offensive in the eye of the world, 1 Sam. 2:17, 30.

items.h: In what may we be injurious to our neighbour's good name?
items.e: By flattering him to his face, Proverbs 28:4; by defaming him behind his back, Psalm 50:20; or by bearing false witness against him in public judicature, Ezek. 22:9.

items.h: What is the evil of flattering our neighbour to his face?
items.e: It tends to foster and foment his pride, and thus to bring on his ruin, Proverbs 26:28 - "A flattering mouth worketh ruin."

items.h: What is the evil of defaming him behind his back?
items.e: Nothing can be more devilish and malicious, than to fix calumny and reproach upon one, when he is not present to vindicate and defend himself: hence the same original word, which is rendered slanderer, 1 Tim. 3:11, is used also to signify the devil, 1 Pet. 5:8.

items.h: Who are they that maybe guilty of bearing false witness against their neighbour in public judicature?
items.e: The prosecutor, defendant, witness, advocate, and judge, may each of them be guilty in this way.

items.h: How may the prosecutor be guilty?
items.e: In making an unjust demand upon the defendant, Acts 24:5; or laying to his charge that of which he believes him to be innocent, chap. 25:7.

items.h: How is the defendant, upon the other hand, chargeable with guilt in this matter?
items.e: By artful and dilatory evasions, by which the plaintiff is put to needless trouble and charge in the obtaining of justice.

items.h: How may witnesses, in public judicature, be injurious to their neighbour's good name?
items.e: Not only by the heinous sin of bearing testimony to a downright falsehood, but likewise by denying, mincing, or keeping back the truth, or any part of it.

items.h: When are advocates or attorneys guilty in this way?
items.e: When they take in hand to plead and maintain a bad cause, looking on it as a part of their profession to be as warm and zealous in defending what is wrong, as what is just and right.

items.h: How may the judge be guilty of bearing false witness?
items.e: By a rash, partial, and iniquitous sentence; thus perverting justice, and injuring the innocent, like Pilate, Matt. 27:24, 26.

items.h: What is the evil of injuring our neighbour in his good name?
items.e: It robs him of a most valuable treasure; for, if once his good name or character is sunk, his further usefulness in the world is, to all appearance, irrecoverably gone.

items.h: What should affright and deter us from the sins of the tongue, forbidden in this commandment?
items.e: That we are to answer, in the last and great day for our words, as well as our actions, Matt. 12:36, 37 - "Every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment; for, by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned."

items.h: Which is the Tenth Commandment?
items.e: The Tenth Commandment is, Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his man-servant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.

items.h: What is required in the Tenth Commandment?
items.e: The Tenth Commandment requireth full contentment with our own condition, with a right and charitable frame of spirit toward our neighbour, and all that is his.

items.h: What is the practice of the Papists with reference to the Tenth Commandment?
items.e: They have; (in some of their formularies,) erased the Second Commandment, because contrary to their image worship; therefore, in order to keep up the number TEN, they split THIS into two, making these words, "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house," to be the ninth; and, "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife," &c. to be the tenth.

items.h: How are they confuted?
items.e: By the words of this commandment (as they are here inserted from Ex. 20:17,) being transposed into a different order in Deut. 5:21; where desiring our neighbour's wife is put before coveting of his house; which is a plain evidence, that what the Papists make two is but one undivided precept; otherwise what, according to them, is the ninth in the one place, will be the tenth in the other.

items.h: What is the general duty required in this commandment?
items.e: It is an inward disposition and inclination of the whole soul, to perform all the duties contained in the law, particularly in the second table, which this commandment more immediately respects; and that out of love to God, and a desire to please him, Psalm 119:5, 47.

items.h: How do you prove this to be the general duty required?
items.e: From the general sin forbidden; namely, COVETOUSNESS, which includes the motion or stirring of corruption against all the commands of the law, because of their holiness and contrariety to depraved nature, Rom. 7:7, 8.

items.h: What inward disposition of soul does this commandment require with reference to ourselves in particular?
items.e: It requires, with reference to ourselves, full contentment with our own condition, 1 Tim. 6:6.

items.h: What do you understand by full contentment with our own condition?
items.e: A cheerful acquiescence in the lot which God, in his holy and wise providence, is pleased to carve out for us in this world, Heb. 13:5 - "Be content with such things as ye have."

items.h: Is full contentment with our own condition attainable in this life?
items.e: Though the perfection of no grace is attainable in this life, yet a great measure, and eminent degrees of grace, particularly this of contentment, may be, and has been, attained by the saints in this world, Phil. 4:11 - "I have learned, in whatever state I am, therewith to be content."

items.h: Is contentment, in a prosperous condition, an easy attainment?
items.e: No; without grace it cannot be attained; because, naturally, our ambitious and covetous desires increase in proportion to our riches; as is evident in the instance of Ahab, whom a kingdom could not satisfy without Naboth's vineyard, 1 Kings 21:4.

items.h: How is true contentment attained under prosperous circumstances?
items.e: By looking above all the enjoyments of time as transitory and vain, to God himself, as our chief good and eternal inheritance, Psalm 62:10, and 16:5, 6.

items.h: Is contentment likewise required under cross dispensations of providence; such as, poverty, reproach, bodily afflictions, and loss of near relations?
items.e: Though it be a grievous sin to be stupidly insensible and unconcerned under these or the like circumstances, Hos. 7:9; yet a contentment of submission, or such as is without repining and murmuring, is, undoubtedly, required under the severest troubles that can befall us in this life, Lam. 3:39 - "Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?" And, Ezra. 9:13 "...seeing that thou our God hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve,"

items.h: What ground of contentment have we under outward poverty and want?
items.e: That, though we be the poor of this world, yet we may be "rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom," James 2:5.

items.h: Why should we bear reproach without murmuring?
items.e: Because whatever reproach is cast upon us for Christ's sake, he will wipe it clean off at his second appearing, Luke 22:28, 29; Matt. 25:34.

items.h: What reason for contentment have we under bodily afflictions?
items.e: That they are only of short duration, 2 Cor. 4:17; mixed with mercy, Lam. 3:32; consistent with love, John 11:3; and designed for "our profit, that we might be partakers of his holiness," Heb. 12:10.

items.h: What should content and comfort us under the loss of near and dear relations?
items.e: That the Lord Jesus, who stands in every amiable relation to us, is always at hand, being "the same yesterday, today, and for ever," Heb. 13:8.

items.h: Are we required to be content under divine desertion, or the want of the sense of the love of God?
items.e: Though we have no reason to quarrel with God, for withdrawing the light of his countenance, which we never deserved; yet it is impossible for any gracious soul to be easy and content under the hidings of his face, but it must needs earnestly long for, and ardently breathe after the returns of his love; as is evident from the example and practice of the saints, in the following texts, Job 23:3, and 29:2, 3; Psalm 13:1, 42:1, 2, and 84:2.

items.h: What inward frame or disposition of soul does the Tenth Commandment require with reference to our neighbour?
items.e: It requires a right and charitable frame of spirit toward him, and all that is his, Rom. 12:16.

items.h: When may we be said to have this right and charitable frame of spirit here required?
items.e: When our inward motions and affections are influenced by grace, to sway and determine us to promote and rejoice in the welfare of our neighbour, both as to his spiritual and temporal concerns, 1 Cor. 13:4-8.

items.h: When may it be evident to ourselves, that we have a right and charitable frame of spirit towards those who excel us in gifts and graces?
items.e: When, under an humbling sense of our own defects, we are thankful for the honour that is brought to God, by the shining of his gifts or graces in others, Gal. 1:23, 24.

items.h: What should induce us to a right and charitable frame of spirit towards those that are in more prosperous circumstances than ourselves; or whose condition in the world is better than our own?
items.e: The considering that a flourishing condition in the world is not always the best, Psalm 38:16; that if we enjoy communion with God, it is infinitely preferable to all outward prosperity without it, Psalm 16:5, 6.

items.h: How may such a right and charitable frame of spirit be attained?
items.e: Only by the implantation of faith, as the root of this and all other motions of the soul that are acceptable to God, Heb. 11:6; Rom. 14:23.

items.h: What is forbidden in the Tenth Commandment?
items.e: The Tenth Commandment forbiddeth all discontentment with our own estate, envying or grieving at the good of our neighbour, and all inordinate motions and affections to any thing that is his.

items.h: What is the leading sin forbidden in this commandment?
items.e: It is COVETOUSNESS: Thou shalt not covet.

items.h: What is covetousness?
items.e: It is an excessive and irregular desire after those worldly goods which we have not, Proverbs 1:19, and which God, in his providence, does not see meet that we should have, Psalm 75:6, 7.

items.h: How does the excess of an avaricious mind discover itself?
items.e: By such an insatiable thirst after worldly gain, as can never be satisfied, Proverbs 30:15.

items.h: In what consists the irregularity of covetousness?
items.e: In the desire of worldly goods which are in the possession of our neighbour, and even sometimes as they are his, 1 Kings 21:2.

items.h: How does the covetousness of the heart discover itself?
items.e: By discontentment with our own estate, and envying or grieving at the good of our neighbour.

items.h: What is discontentment with our own estate?
items.e: It is to murmur and fret at our present condition in the world, as being worse than we think should fall to our share, or than we are expecting and looking for, 2 Kings 6:33.

items.h: What is the aggravation of this sin?
items.e: It argues an unwillingness to be at God's disposal, Psalm 12:4; an esteeming ourselves more competent judges than he, of what is best for us, 1 Kings 1:5; and it is, in effect, usurping the throne of God, and taking his government into our own hands, Ex. 5:2.

items.h: What are the proper remedies against it?
items.e: The only sovereign remedy, is to give Christ the pre-eminence in our hearts, Psalm 73:25; for then we will undervalue all temporal things, in comparison of him, Psalm 76:4.

items.h: What is envying or grieving at the good of our neighbour?
items.e: It is to repine and grudge at his prosperous circumstances, Neh. 2:10, or any superior endowment or privilege he is possessed of above ourselves, Psalm 112:9, 10.

items.h: What is the evil of this sin?
items.e: It wastes and consumes the body, Proverbs 14:30 - "Envy is the rottenness of the bones," and it is fertile of "confusion, and every evil work," James 3:16.

items.h: What is the source or spring of covetousness?
items.e: The inordinate motions and affections that are in our souls.

items.h: What do you understand by the inordinate motions and affections here forbidden?
items.e: Not only the unlawful purposes, intentions, and desires, that are actually formed in the heart, but even the first risings and stirrings of corruption in the soul, which are antecedent to the consent of the will, Gen. 6:5.

items.h: Are not the vicious lusts and desires that are, formed and assented to in the heart, forbidden in other commandments of the second table, as well as in this?
items.e: Yes; as appears from our Saviour's exposition of the Seventh Commandment, Matt. 5:28 - "But I say unto you, Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her, hath committed adultery with her already in his heart."

items.h: How then is this commandment distinguished from others, which forbid heart sins equally with it?
items.e: This commandment is levelled particularly at the root of all sin, namely, habitual lust, or corruption of nature, together with its very first motions, and especially as these are contrary to the love of our neighbour; whereas, other commandments chiefly respect such secret and heart sins as are actually committed, though not known to the world.

items.h: How does it appear that this commandment is levelled particularly at habitual lust, or at the root of all sin?
items.e: Because, since other commandments chiefly forbid heart sins actually formed, this commandment must forbid the very rise of them, or the least bias and inclination to evil; otherwise it would not be distinct from the rest, nor would the law be absolutely perfect.

items.h: Does not the apostle James distinguish between lust and sin, chap. 1:15 - "When lust hath conceived it bringeth forth sin;" and will it not from thence follow, that lust, or corruption of nature, is not properly sin, and consequently not forbidden in this commandment?
items.e: The apostle distinguishes between lust and sin merely as a corrupt principle and the act which it produces; both which are hateful to God, and contrary to his law.

items.h: If lust, or corruption of nature, cannot be remedied, or extirpated by any prescription in the Divine law, why is it at all prohibited?
items.e: It is nevertheless prohibited, both because contrary to the nature of God, and as a mean to reprove and humble us for it, Rom. 7:9.

items.h: What is the difference between human and Divine laws on this head?
items.e: Human laws respect only overt or open acts of sin, but Divine laws respect likewise the internal inclination and disposition which persons have to commit it, Psalm 66:18.
